The first topic deals with the goods and services tax. The petitioners from Kamloops and Chase, British Columbia are totally distressed with the government's continued determination to proceed with this 7 per cent goods and services tax and are calling upon the Liberals in the Senate to stop it.

maintopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT

maintopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext: Actually, it is not what the petition says, Mr. Speaker, but it is what they are thinking. If I can be so bold to presume what the petitioners are actually hoping for, it is that the Liberal senators who dominate the Senate will vote it down this afternoon and end this threat.

maintopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT

They came from every community, from Baie-Sainte-Anne, Escuminac, all the fishing communities of Kent County, from Westmorland County, even as far as Cape Tormentine.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the duty to table a petition that follows the example of several thousand Canadians who are protesting strongly against the Conservative government's proposal to impose upon Canadians a further tax on the goods and services that they purchase starting January 1.
These Canadians-and there are hundreds of signatures in this petition-would like to state without a doubt their strong objection to the imposition of this unprecedented tax. The petitioners would also like to state that in their opinion it is an unjustified grab from the pockets of Canadians which will hit them not only with a higher tax load but with higher inflation, higher interest rates, and higher unemployment.
The undersigned humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject the proposed goods and services tax.

speechtext: In the summer of 1989, did officials of Forestry Canada state that there were administrative problems in paying contractors for tree planting, and, if so, have any steps been taken taken to correct these problems and, if so, what steps?

speakeroldname: The Hon. Frank Oberle (Minister of Forestry):
maintopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS DISSOLUTION OR TRANSFER AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
During the summer of 1989, the British Columbia Employment Standards Branch (Prince George office) received a number of complaints from tree planters. These complaints reflected an abnormal occurrence, due to the dissolution of a company in June 1989.
In 1989, Forestry Canada officials (Pacific and Yukon Region) investigated issues regarding tree planting administration under the Canada-British Columbia Forest Resource Development Agreement (FRDA).
It would be very difficult to relate the complaints generated by the dissolution of a company directly to administrative practices under the Canada-British Columbia FRDA. It was determined that administrative problems did not exist under the BC FRDA and, therefore, no changes were made to the administrative process.
Although the implementation of cost-shared programs under the FRDA and their adherence to the employment standards is within the jurisdiction of the provincial government, the federal government has advocated that the working and safety conditions of silviculture workers be improved.
The FRDA created much employment for silviculture workers in 1989, generating an estimated 14,000 person-days of employment to plant some 19 million seedlings on 7,000 hectares in the Prince George Region. However, with the exception of the one company which failed, the proportion of complaints to the Employment Standards Branch does not appear to be unusual.

That this Chamber, recognizing the historical events taking place in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, regretting the lack of clear policy by the government in defining a new Canadian role in response to these events, noting the failure to address the serious issues of trade, commercial relations, Arctic security and agriculture agreements, and the confusion between the Minister of National Defence and Secretary of State on NATO, calls upon the government through open parliamentary consultations to develop independent, effective policy initiatives in foreign policy and trade to meet these new conditions.
He said: Mr. Speaker, today the Official Opposition takes this opportunity to present a motion of censure because we regret it has now become common practice to develop Canada's foreign policy on the sly, often without any public consultation, a policy that also seems more inclined to take its cue from our neighbours to the south, reflecting American interests instead of representing a genuinely Canadian position.
I may remind hon. members of the first meeting in Quebec City between Mr. Reagan and Mr. Mulroney, when our Prime Minister launched the initiative for negotiations on the free trade agreement with the United States, without prior consultation with the Canadian public. Worse, Canadians were constantly kept in the dark about developments in the course of these negotiations with the Americans, allegedly because we could not reveal our strategy and objectives to our economic partners.
The Americans knew exactly where they were going and had no qualms about saying so publicly, even tabling their action plan in the U.S. Congress. In fact, they were very successful, since they got us to abolish the Foreign Investment Review Agency, for their sake. We passed legislation that was favourable to their big drug companies. They obtained the deregulation of the transportation industry, which we now realize is heavily weighted in favour of American truckers and American railway companies. They obtained a guarantee from Canada that the U.S. could always count on access to our natural resources. Finally, they obtained the gradual phasing-

May 31, 1990

out of all subsidy programs for Canadian companies and farmers. That is what they wanted and that is what they got. Unfortunately, we cannot say the picture is as rosy on our side. According to the Prime Minister, our main goal was to have guaranteed access to the U.S. market.
That was not achieved since we are still subject to retaliatory measures by the U.S. Congress. Now there is talk about a United States-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement, and it seems that negotiations will be starting very soon between the Americans and the Mexicans, our government also wants to get involved. Here again, there were no prior consultations, not even with our parliamentary committee, and certainly not with the Canadian public. In any case, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre will expand on this question later on in the debate today, when he will also mention other negative aspects of Canada's international trade policies.
I may recall, Mr. Speaker, that our Prime Minister decided that Canada would become a member of the Organization of American States, following his first meeting with President Bush. This decision took everybody by surprise. No one expected it, not even officials at the Department of External Affairs, who did not see this as a priority and who were not and still are not ready to tackle this new priority since they lack the budgets and staff to deal with the new responsibilities tossed their way by the Prime Minister, en route to Costa Rica.
What the Liberal Party of Canada said at the time is unfortunately, still true today. The Liberal Party feels that Canada's membership should have been subject to the following conditions: First, membership should not be a substitute for a valid policy in the region. The Mulroney government should make a formal commitment, through concrete action, to enhancing Canada's presence in Latin America and the Caribbean, both in the form of financial and human resources. Second, the government should start by formulating a set of priorities and principles to guide the activities of Canadian representatives at the OAS and in the region. For example, strongly promote respect for human rights and closely monitor situations that might lead to violations of these rights; provide effective aid, taking account of respect for human rights and the environment; increase efforts to solve the debt crisis, especially by restoring to their former level contributions to the Inter-American Development Bank and the Caribbean Development Bank; clearly state Canada's point of view on the settlement of
conflicts in the region and promote the democratization of institutions and governments.
I must say that the government has not done much so far to meet these conditions.
Finally, the Minister of External Affairs, in a speech he gave at Humber College in Toronto on the weekend, just set forth Canada's new policy on Europe. Again, Mr. Speaker, there was no public consultation and the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade was not consulted either.
That is quite insulting, because since last September, the members of this committee have been dealing with the new situation in Europe following the political events in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe and especially with the emergence of the single market in Europe in 1992. We held hundreds of meetings and heard dozens of witnesses representing the opinions of Canadian and foreign experts on this subject. We have returned from a trip to observe and study the Soviet Union and East and West Germany and we are preparing to publish the results of our work in the coming days.
Now the minister, before this report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade is made public, tells us his new policy and rejects outright all these suggestions that may have been useful to him. I understand his not wanting the ideas and opinions of opposition members, but I remind him that over half a dozen members of his own party worked with us on these recommendations; they are being treated quite cavalierly and incorrectly by the minister.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I read the minister's speech and that I find it incredibly trite in some respects.
Having reminded us that, at Montreal's McGill University on February 5, he announced his intention to re-examine our European policy with a view to defining Canada's interests in that part of the world and implementing a strategy to serve these interests, he now states solemnly that, since trade accounts for 30 per cent of our GNP, the unification of the Western European market is of the utmost importance for Canadian employment and prosperity and that the huge untapped markets of Eastern Europe may also prove to be veiy promising in the long term.
Mr. Speaker, he did not really have to wait nearly four months to say that. Besides, I would suggest that his conclusions concerning NATO are unduly conservative.

Acknowledging as he does, that it is only natural that NATO should play a more political role which would mirror Europe's new reality and its declining military mission, and that NATO must seek security through arms control with as much energy as it sought security through military deployment, the minister concludes by saying that a strong military mandate for NATO is still valid and that the presence of Canadian and American troops in Europe remains essential.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, our commitment towards Europe does not necessarily call for our military presence over there and, in that respect, the government will have to take a much more enlightened approach.
Speaking objectively, I must say the minister's proposals for the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe are interesting and certainly deserve to be vigorously promoted by Canada.
However, the minister also made a vague reference to a CSCE assembly of parliamentarians. I would have preferred to hear more about the European Council. I wish the minister would announce that Canada will apply for membership in the European Council and I that he will work on making the European Council the parliamentary wing of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe.
The minister also said solemnly: "Our interests in Europe are real, contemporary and imperative". Well said, but I may remind him there is a lack of resources. His department has been asked to scale down, and the Minister of Finance is putting tremendous pressure on his department to reduce spending. I think he may be biting off more than he can chew. How can the minister expect his diplomats to be everywhere at once? After all, they are only human.
The minister has just given us a major action plan for ensuring our future presence in Europe. I am afraid those objectives will not be met if we treat Europe the same way we treated the fourteen bilateral agreements signed by Mr. Mulroney in Moscow last November.
I think it is clear their operations are on hold, and I deplore the government's total lack of initiative and failure to do any follow-up on these issues. The Liberal Party of Canada issued a press release on the occasion of

President Gorbachev's visit to Ottawa, and I would like to quote a few paragraphs:
The Liberals feel that Canada can be of invaluable assistance in supporting President Gorbachev's efforts to reorganize the Soviet economy, provide for a more democratic political system and revitalize Soviet society.
Our diplomatic presence in that country is a tangible symbol of Canada's commitment in this respect. However, this presence is not equal to the task. We are sorry to see that the Government of Canada has yet to open a new consulate in Kiev, and we deplore the fact that there is no consulate in Leningrad.
We want to ask the Conservative Government to provide for a significant increase in the number of diplomats posted to Moscow. The present staff of fewer than 20 is not adequate, considering the very demanding aspects of Canadian-Soviet relations, and the impression is given that Canadian-Soviet relations are not a priority with the Conservative Govement.
The Liberals feel this is an intolerable situation that should be corrected as soon as possible.
In 1984, the previous Liberal government, under the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, signed an unprecedented agreement for scientific co-operation in the Arctic with the Soviet Union. The Liberals are happy to see that further agreements on co-operation in the Arctic were signed when the Prime Minister visited Moscow last November.
As we said earlier, however, we are disappointed because implementation of these agreements is lagging, and we urge the minister to take steps to advance this dossier. We also regret that the Mulroney government is reluctant to engage in serious talks with the Soviet Union on security in the Arctic and arms limitation.
Since 1988, we have proposed a multilateral arms limitation system for the Arctic, and as Liberals, we once again ask the Mulroney government to respond to Soviet indications of interest in arms limitation in the Arctic.
Liberal Parliamentarians who recently visited the USSR were quite concerned when they learned that that country was planning to re-locate its nuclear test field in the Arctic as of 1995.
We strongly urge President Gorbachev to publically refute entertaiming such a notion which we feel would jeopardize the Arctic's already fragile environment and which is certainly not consistent with the statements he has made himself on the opportunity to demilitarize the Arctic and to sign a general nuclear test ban treaty.
I suggest this is one of the main items in our relations with the USSR and I ask the Minister to make every effort to convince Soviet leaders to change their mind.

I need not tell you that we no longer have a defence policy. The White Paper tabled by the Minister of Defence is no longer relevant. It is just a pile of paper which the government has simply thrown into the waste basket. But it has done nothing to develop a new defence policy for Canada.
It is also true of the White Paper on international development which has never been implemented by this Tory government. Our international commitments to the Third World are nothing to be proud of and fall short of the proverbial generosity of Canadians.
In a little while, my colleague the hon. member for Northumberland will discuss in greater detail how this government has sold out the various groups of Canadians operating in under-developed countries and how two-faced the Tories have been in connection with the most blatant violations of human rights by several governments which are recipients of Canadian foreign aid.
Mr. Speaker, Canada is a member of the UN Security Council. Regretfully, it uses its position on the council with extreme caution. So much so that we can rightfully wonder if the government realizes that we have a major role to play and that we have the responsibility to present the Security Council with original, independent and somewhat liberal initiatives. That is what this government should do and is not doing.
That is why we have moved today this motion blaming the government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to discuss foreign policy in the House, although I confess to some puzzlement of both the timing and the content of the motion and indeed, some of the references of my good friend, the spokesman for the Liberal party.
The motion was about Europe. He spent a good part of his time talking about the United States. My colleague from Etobicoke-Lakeshore suggested perhaps we
should send him a map. Obviously, relations with the United States are important, but I want to make a point to my good friend. The world is larger than the United States. This government has focused our foreign policy on the recognition that, as important as our relationship might be with our neighbour, we have a larger world in which we have to work. That has been a motive of our policy.
This motion alleges a lack of "effective policy initiatives in foreign policy". Yet, in just the last seven days, Canada has welcomed the Secretary-General of the United Nations, who came specifically to express his appreciation of Canada's contribution to that most central of the world's organizations. The vice-president of the European communities was here as part of a deliberate process of high level meetings between the Community and Canada, initiated by the government. Also we hosted the first visit to Canada in 19 years by a leader of the Soviet Union.
The world is changing dramatically-in the Soviet Union, in Europe, in South Africa, in Central America, in Cambodia, in Mexico, in Latin America at large-and Canada is pursuing an active, effective and distinctively Canadian foreign policy on each of those fronts. We will welcome suggestions from other parties as to other initiatives we should consider, but we do that against the background of a foreign policy which I am proud to defend anywhere in Canada, or the world.
Let me deal briefly with the reference to parliamentary consultations. I think governments traditionally make too little use of members of Parliament in foreign policy, and we have tried to change that practice. We will consider any serious proposals members might make as to how the role can be enlarged. I have just received my invitation from the standing committee to go before it to discuss the results of its deliberations. I actually look forward to doing that.
I have to note, Mr. Speaker, last week when I went before the committee, the hon. member was asking me why I was late in announcing my policy. Today, he asks me why I announced it so early. Also, I want to indicate an area in which he and I are solidly in agreement. He tells me that the diplomats in my department are overworked. They are overworked, but they are hardy

May 31, 1990

people with great imagination, ingenuity and dedication to the country.
We believe, even in this period of limited resources, we have the capacities to be effective on a wide variety of fronts. If the hon. member is suggesting that the Liberal party has a list of issues from which Canada should back away, I would be prepared to look at that list but not, I must say, with a great deal of sympathy.
It was in the spirit of consultation with parliamentarians that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and I met this morning with colleagues who had just returned from a visit to AECL facilities in Romania. As I said, I have accepted enthusiastically to meet members of the standing committee to discuss their recent trip to the Soviet Union. I can report to the House that last week the standing committee asked me if there could be increased contact between Canadian and Soviet parliamentarians to discuss Arctic matters.
I made that proposal to Mr. Shevardnadze on Tuesday, and he agreed immediately. This will augment the very active co-operation that is already in place including, in part as a result of discussions in the standing committee, a discussion of the implications, environmental and otherwise, of the shifting of a greater degree of Soviet nuclear testing into Arctic regions. I am prepared to act with similar dispatch on other practical proposals that colleagues might make.
Five central issues were discussed in the meetings by the Prime Minister, the Deputy Prime Minister and myself with President Gorbachev, Mr. Shevardnadze and the Soviet Deputy Chairman of the Council of Ministers, Mr. Maslukov.
First, was the high priority both countries assigned to enlarging our co-operation as neighbours and as nations sharing a widening range of common interests. The mutual priority is demonstrated by the fact that in the last seven months the Prime Minister and Mr. Gorbachev have held two sets of long, personal, face-to-face discussions. Mr. Shevardnadze has visited Canada for consultations twice in this period; in February and again in May. I have accepted his invitation to return to Moscow this fall to maintain that momentum.
Second, Canada affirmed our strong support of the profound economic and political reforms in the Soviet Union and discussed practical ways in which Canada can
Supply
help in changing COCOM rules, in helping boost Soviet integration into the world economic system by more joint ventures to add to the 35 that have already been signed between Canadians and Soviets, by attractive arrangements to encourage immediate delivery of Canadian agricultural products and by the discussion of new agreements regarding fisheries, tourism, health and potentially, educational exchanges.
Third, we made the case that it contributes to stability throughout Europe to have a united Germany that is actively involved in institutions like NATO and the European Community. But we heard and we understand the case, that the Soviets need to see evidence of changes in NATO before they will believe that institution is adapting to the new realities of Europe. As the Prime Minister said yesterday, Canada will work to ensure that Article 2 of NATO, the political article originally proposed by Canada, becomes much more central to NATO.
Fourth, we discussed in detail measures which Canada and the Soviet Union agree to strengthen the process and the relevance of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. Our two nations are on the outer ends of Europe. We have a special interest and we have a common interest in developing strong institutions that define and unite a large Europe from Vladivostok to Vancouver Island.
Finally, the Prime Minister and I both raised the serious situation in the Baltic states, and repeated our expectation that there would not be a crackdown, and that the issues whose sensitivity everyone acknowledges, will be resolved by negotiation. I welcomed Mr. Shevardnadze's assurance that the Soviet Union intends to seek political solutions to disagreements, whether those relate to matters they consider to be internal or external.

Mr. Speaker, 1989 was a year of revolution in Europe, and 1990 marks the beginning of reconstruction. New societies and new institutions must be built now, and that is just starting.
The 1989 revolution produced fundamental repercussions on all of the European continent and North America as well. Indeed, by its language, family and historical ties, our continent is a reflection of Europe

May 31, 1990
Supply
across the Atlantic. That is why our government has undertaken a review of our policy concerning Europe.
Canada's interest for Europe is not motivated solely by historical reasons, nostalgia or the desire to be charitable. What is at stake is not only the prosperity of Europe, but ours as well.
However, our ways of pursuing those interests must change radically in order to reflect the new security environment which is emerging, the ever-increasing authority and unity of Western Europe as well as Canada's unique assets.
The link between us and Europe has been our contribution to the North Atlantic Alliance. That contribution involved stationing in Germany thousands of Canadian servicemen and women who have risk their lives daily in the name of freedom.
Our military contribution is bound to decrease.
The organization whose primary role has been to protect us against potential agression has to re-examine its role when such an agression becomes less likely. Under those circumstances, it is only natural for NATO to take on a more political role reflecting the new realities of Europe and a waning military one.
Canada fully supports such a change. It serves Canadian interests.

NATO must review urgently and comprehensively all aspects of its nuclear and conventional strategy. It makes little sense to retain those short-range nuclear weapons based in Europe whose only target can be our new friends in Poland, in Czechoslovakia, and in East Germany. It makes little sense to maintain a military strategy which is based on a scenario of a surprise attack across a front which no longer exists and where surprise is no longer possible. It makes little sense to continue to retain in Europe the largest peacetime deployment of military force in the history of the world.
This is not to deny the continuing requirement for prudence and for military stability at this time of historic change. The possibility of instability is there and Soviet military capacities remain substantial. Therefore, a strong military mandate for NATO continues to be valid and the North American commitment to Europe, represented by the presence of Canadian and American
troops there is crucial as we strive for strategic stability at significantly lower levels of military force.
It is important that NATO become even more actively engaged in the dynamic new security dialogue.
In the field of arms controls and disarmament, NATO should develop an enhanced capacity and role in confidence-building and verification activities. Dedicated multinational forces on the ground might be deployed for this purpose. NATO should also look to the establishment of a verification centre to co-ordinate those activities.
In addition, NATO should move away from a rigid forward defence to a much more flexible approach involving mobile units, possibly including forces of a multinational nature.
NATO is of enduring value. But it has its limitations, a function of its mandate and its membership. There are other institutions whose role must be enhanced and transformed.
Central among those is the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. Its membership is comprehensive, encompassing the nations of Europe, North America and the Soviet Union. Its mandate extends across the board.
The role of the CSCE must now be expanded so that it becomes the drawing-board for the new European architecture. As a complement to NATO, the CSCE can become a true instrument of co-operative security, one which would supplement deterrence with reassurance.
Until now, the CSCE has lacked the institutional framework now required for effective and ongoing cooperation and confidence-building.
Canada believes that continuing political direction from the highest level is required. Canada proposes that the CSCE should meet annually at the level of Foreign Ministers and every two years at the level of heads of government. This political body could serve as the beginnings of a council for European co-operation, a future permanent forum for dialogue on pan-European questions.
The CSCE should develop a forum to reflect the increasingly democratic character of its membership. Therefore, we also proposed the establishment of a CSCE assembly where parliamentary delegations from
May 31, 1990

member states would meet on a regular basis to discuss issues of common concern.
In the security area, the CSCE will have a role in mandating a further round of conventional forces reduction talks. These talks should be conducted among all 35 members of the CSCE, rather than solely the members of NATO and the Warsaw treaty organizations.
The CSCE should also increase its role in verification and confidence-building, and in crisis prevention and conflict resolution. This could involve the creation of a mechanism to facilitate dialogue, to conduct fact-finding investigations if required and to recommend a strategy to resolve crises, whether it be mediation, arbitration or even peacekeeping. If the crisis develops into conflict, the CSCE should initiate mediation activities. These activities could be supported by a permanent institute for the peaceful settlement of disputes which could provide very valuable expertise.
Beyond the security field, the CSCE should build upon the other principles contained in the Helsinki Agreements. The essential structures of democracy should become a common commitment of CSCE members, including the right to free elections and the rule of law. Pluralism should also be legitimized throughout the CSCE process, as should the rights of minorities, freedom of religion and a prohibition on hate propaganda.
In the economic dimension, the CSCE may also have a valuable role in the future, building on the tremendous success of the recent Bonn Economic Conference. It was a success, by the way, because of the participation of a wide range of Canadians, including prominently those from the private sector, who made an important contribution. It should not duplicate existing and effective economic institutions. But there is room for growth in encouraging co-operation and dialogue. I believe a permanent CSCE forum for economic dialogue, supplementing the emerging work in the OECD, is worth very serious consideration.
NATO and the CSCE are complementary institutions in building the new Europe. But there is another institution, the European Community, which is central to Europe's future identity and prosperity.

The European Community is now a welcome and fundamental pillar of the international system. A uniting Europe is an engine of prosperity and a trigger to enhanced trade. Increasing co-operation in the political field and, eventually, the security fields will ensure European consensus and co-ordination in ways which can only enhance international stability.
But, Mr. Speaker, a wall dividing Europe cannot be supplanted by a wall around Europe. Two impermeable blocs cannot be replaced by one new bloc which, whether in trade or security or political matters, is less open to dialogue and co-operation than it is today. The new Europe must be an open Europe, open to the west and open to the east.
Of course, Canada is not a member of the European Community. But we are a trading nation. We have a profound interest in the questions of foreign policy which are increasingly the subject of European political co-operation.
It is for this reason that Canada is now proposing a new, more intense relationship between Canada and the European Community. We are proposing regular meetings between the Prime Minister of Canada and the President of the European Council. These should be supplemented by regular in-depth discussions between the Canadian Foreign Minister and the Foreign Minister of each incoming presidency. There should also be regular meetings between experts on issues of common concern. In addition, we propose that there be an exchange of priorities at the beginning of each presidency which would set the agenda for the upcoming period.
Finally, I was very attracted by the proposal made by West German Minister Hans Dietrich Genscher for an EEC-North American declaration which would confirm shared principles and interests in openness and enhanced co-operation. Mr. Genscher made that proposal when he was recently here in Ottawa. Certainly, a broad reaffirmation of the trans-Atlantic relationship would, in our judgment, be useful.
In trade, the challenge for Canada is acute. The government has already announced its Europe 1992 strategy to help Canadian industry prepare for the opportunity and the demands which the single European

May 31, 1990
Supply
market will present to all traders. However, I also believe there may be virtue at the conclusion of the Uruguay Round of trade negotiations in examining the desirability of a formalized, open trading agreement between Canada and the European Community, perhaps including the United States-or indeed other members of the OECD. We think that would be something worth considering at the end of the Uruguay Round.
A new direction for NATO, an expanded role for the CSCE and an intensified relationship with the European Economic Community-those are the institutional pillars of our new policy toward Europe.
But our policy toward Europe hinges, as does the future of the new Europe itself, on the continued success of the reforms now under way in the Soviet Union and in eastern Europe. Those reforms have a long way to go before promise becomes reality.
That, Sir, if I may say, is part of the reason that it was so important that the public reaction that was evident in the streets of this capital city when Mr. Gorbachev was here sent a message of encouragement and support from the ordinary people of Canada to a man who is undertaking extraordinary and extraordinarily difficult reforms.
When you think of it, the task of simultaneously constructing democracy and an open-market economy, and doing it from the ground up is unprecedented. The west has an abiding interest in seeing the east succeed. That is why Canada has actively supported Soviet integration into the western economic system. That is why the Prime Minister has proposed and other leaders have accepted that the chairman of each Summit meeting will debrief Mr. Gorbachev. That is why we have helped them achieve observer status in the GATT, and why we are looking at other ways in which they can become part of the international economic system. That is why Mr. Shevardnadze thanked me yesterday for Canada's support for Soviet membership in the new European Bank and our support for their observer status in the GATT. That is why, last year, we established a program to assist Poland and Hungary in their efforts at economic reform.
It is time for the international effort, focusing in the first instance on Poland and Hungary, to expand to include the other new democracies emerging from the
European revolution of 1989. In the weeks ahead, the 24 countries which co-ordinated the program for Hungary and Poland will meet to broaden that effort to include these other countries. Canada will support that initiative. We will announce our own expanded national program in the short term. Canada is also participating fully in the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
Finally, we have established a Task Force on Central and Eastern Europe which will elaborate the details of our expanded assistance program, administer that program and co-ordinate private and public sector activities. This task force has begun an intensive series of consultations with Canadian groups and individuals, encouraging them to participate financially and in practical, concrete ways-and asking them for their advice on initiatives we might undertake.
Assistance to eastern Europe is not a matter of dumping large amounts of money into the hands of these new governments. What is more important and more effective is the provision of expertise, the training of managers, the training of decision-makers, the teaching of the tools of democracy and the encouragement of private sector investment in specific projects and enterprises.
In this task Canada has an asset available to no other nation. We have our multicultural community. One in ten Canadians is of Soviet or eastern European ancestry. They are a business asset. They are a trading asset for Canada. They know the customs. They know the decision-makers. They know the systems. They know the languages.
We want these Canadians to exercise their natural advantages, to tell us how we can help and how we can do what we do better-and to pursue this opportunity of a lifetime.
The policy I have outlined today addresses a Europe in transition. The policy itself must also evolve with the region it addresses. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss with members of the standing committee their specific proposals as to how that evolution should occur.
Europe is not static, and neither will Canadian policy be static.
May 31, 1990

Engagement with the new Europe is not a luxury for Canada; it is a necessity for Canada. Canada will be there, as we must, for our own sake, for our own security and for our own prosperity.

Did the minister raise the issue of current severe shortage of medical supplies in Lithuania? And could the minister tell us whether the Soviet authorities are prepared to let Canada ship drugs, hypodermics and all kinds of medical equipment that seem to be in very short supply at the present time?

I have a question on this matter, Mr. Speaker.
The minister repeated the assertion that he has received from Mr. Shevardnadze on a number of occasions that there will be no crackdown.
The point I would like to have the minister respond to is: At what point does a blockade become just another form of a crackdown? It is one thing not to hit people over the head or employ military force, but if at some point they cannot heat their homes, refrigerate their food; if diabetics cannot get insulin; if people who need operations cannot have them, particularly if they are life-saving operations; and if there is a threat of infection, indeed even of epidemic proportion, then this surely must be called a crackdown of a different sort.
I would encourage the government to be as forceful as possible in saying that we, as a country, are not accepting the view that just because there is no military crackdown nothing unacceptable has happened.
I know that the government has protested the blockade, et cetera. I am just saying that it does become a bit strange after a while to be accepting their assurances about a crackdown while, at the same time, knowing what is going on.
I have been in communication with the Minister of Health in Lithuania and with another Lithuanian official from the health department who was here this week. The situation is becoming critical. No one has died yet as a result of these shortages, but this will happen if the blockade is not lifted or if it is not selectively lifted.
If the Soviets want to impress upon the Lithuanians their dependence on Soviet oil, that is one thing, but to create a situation in which diabetics cannot even get proper medication, proper needles, et cetera, is another thing altogether. It is bringing into disrepute the Soviet position with respect to its not wanting to do anything unacceptable in Lithuania.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question. I know the hon. member in phrasing it, is concerned both to encourage satisfactory development in Lithuania and allow the Soviet Union to maintain the process of reform, something which he so actively supports.
I would make three comments. I agree absolutely that what we are seeking are undertakings of substance, not of semantics.
I cannot answer the question he poses as to when a crackdown becomes a crackdown, but the comments that I made were in the spirit of his question in the House.
Second, I regard it as quite significant that when I raised with Mr. Shevardnadze the concern that had been expressed to me about medical supplies, he said, quite clearly, that there would be no problem with Canadians sending to hospitals, anywhere in the Soviet Union medical supplies where needed. Naturally, I intend to follow that.
As I said to my colleague for Papineau-Saint-Michel, I was also encouraged by the fact that he then went a step further. He said that in the nature of a problem of this kind between the Soviet Union and Lithuania there are going to be other concerns that arise in a country like ours. He gave me his undertaking that he would work personally with me, when those matters were drawn to our attention, first, to see if we could agree that they are serious and, second, if they were, to try to resolve those kinds of obstacles.
Finally, the third point I would like to make on this issue is simply an impression that I have received. It is an impression that I think also reflects some of the public comments of Prime Minister Prunskiene after her meetings with Mr. Gorbachev. I think there is a profound agreement between the leaders of Lithuania and of the Soviet Union on the importance of the reforms the Gorbachev regime has undertaken. Mrs. Prunskiene is among their most active supporters. There is a recognition of a very real dilemma.
My impression-and I can only give it as an impression from the comments I had from the discussions the Prime Minister had with Mr. Gorbachev-is that the Soviets are looking here for some time in which this can be
resolved. I found it interesting that yesterday at the airport Mr. Gorbachev made reference to the situation in Caledonia and the fact that that was a situation which evolved over a decade, that it did not evolve in 40 minutes or in a day. I think it is important that we seek further assurances that that is indeed the perspective in which they are approaching the evolution of Lithuania, but if it is, I think that is a far more hopeful sign than others we thought we had seen in recent days.
I hope that we can all maintain as close a co-operation on this issue as we have.

I would just like to ask what transpired in the discussions over the last few days with our friends from the Soviet Union with respect to grain sales and the grain contracts that will be forthcoming in July, I think it is, of this year. They are so important to the area the minister represents. They are so important to the St. Lawrence Seaway which is a vital transportation link in this country, and they are so important to the ports of Thunder Bay which are perennial winners in these contracts with our friends from the Soviet Union.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity today to speak to this particular motion. It gives us a rare opportunity to talk at length about Canadian foreign policy in the House. In that respect I would like to begin by commenting on some of the claims made about consultation with members of Parliament or the lack thereof when it comes to the making of foreign policy.
I feel that the minister himself has had an intention, only partially realized, to bring members of Parliament more into the debate on foreign policy and also to take the House more seriously than some previous ministers of foreign policy we have known who tended not to make statements in the House in the way this minister has.
The fact remains that the external affairs committee, and Parliament in general, were seriously and justly aggrieved by the way in which the policy with respect to joining the OAS was arrived at, basically by executive decision with no parliamentary consultation whatsoever. I think what complaints we have as parliamentarians and as an external affairs committee come largely out of that experience and the knowledge that we are confronting a government which has the capacity simply to make a major foreign policy decision just like that, without ever even coming to ask us what we think about it at all. That remains an outstanding grievance.

The part of the motion that I would like to address myself to first, has to do with a confusion in government policy that I think I have been a part of and may even be partly responsible for in terms of the questions I have asked in the House. That has to do with the confusion between what the Secretary of State for External Affairs appears to be saying about certain kinds of nuclear weapons in Europe and what the Minister of National Defence has said to me in the House just recently about the same matter.
Going from memory with respect to the minister's speech last Saturday, and he repeated it again today, he said: "Does it make much sense any more to have these short-range nuclear weapons which can only be aimed at the peoples of the new democracies in eastern Europe?"
This is a claim and a question shared by a lot of parliamentarians, including myself and many Canadians. It seems to me that when that kind of question is raised in the House we would be much more confident that what the Secretary of State for External Affairs says reflects government policy if the Minister of National Defence did not pour cold water on the idea and instead said something like "Yes, this is something that we see the logic of and we are considering" and so on, instead of giving us the standard NATO line about the mix of weapons that has kept the peace for 45 years, et cetera. You know the lines as well as anyone else.
What we are trying to establish here is whether this is now something that the government is seriously considering? It seems to me that the government, in doing so, could address some of the concerns that the minister has raised here today and some of the concerns that the Prime Minister raised in his speech yesterday in the presence of Mr. Gorbachev, when he spoke about the Soviet Union's security concerns and particularly the nature of and the future of NATO.
One of the ways in which the west, in this case, with some Canadian leadership could demonstrate to the Soviet Union that NATO is on its way either to becoming something else or on its way out, whatever the case may be, would be to make a decision, in this case a Canadian

Canada should be in a position to say that this is something that we do not want to be a part of anymore because we have made the decision that the appropriate signals need to be sent to the Soviet Union and we want the low-level flight training that exists in Labrador over Innu territory to stop now.
Also, Mr. Speaker, with respect to NATO I would like to address the question of Germany in NATO. I listened
carefully to what the minister had to say and it seems to me again that the signal that needs to be sent with respect to NATO is that NATO, to the extent that it continues to exist, exists in transition. That is why I was concerned when the minister said that NATO is of enduring value. I do not think any institution is of enduring value, except the church. Nothing else is of enduring value this side of the eschaton. So we should talk about NATO to the extent to which it ought to endure for particular purposes until such time as it can be absorbed into the new security architecture of Europe of which the minister spoke.
In that respect I do not accept the analysis that the CSCE and NATO are complementary institutions. I would have preferred to have heard the minister talking about the CSCE being one of the fora in which we will discover or create or agree upon the new architecture into which NATO will finally be absorbed and eventually disappear as we now know it.
It is a mistake to keep talking about NATO as a complementary or enduring institution without setting it in the context of a process by which you see it evolving into something else or evolving out of existence, because we do not even have the Warsaw Pact anymore, for all intents and purposes.
I would like to refer back to Germany, Mr. Speaker. As I have said before in the House, I think it is a mistake to discuss Germany by asking whether it should be neutral or whether it should it be part of NATO, because both of these ways of speaking about Germany assume a divided Europe. They are both captive to cold war language and cold war thinking in the sense that neutrality means being neutral between some opposite poles. This is what the language of neutrality assumes.
I think this is something that the Soviets have to think about too. It assumes the continuation of some form of polarization in Europe for a long time to come. To talk about Germany in NATO also assumes that same bipolarity. So both these ways of speaking are captive to post-war language. We are looking for post post-war language.
This, again, raises the whole debate about NATO, and about having a Germany in NATO. I accept the argument that it is in everyone's interest not to have a Germany sort of freelancing it economically and politically in Europe. We need to talk about the
May 31, 1990

institutionalization of the new Germany within a wider European context. I do not think that can be done within NATO itself unless we are talking about a radically different NATO, or a NATO that is on its way to becoming something altogether different, a NATO that is on its way to being absorbed into some other common security structure for Europe, whether it is Vaclav Havel's European peace order or Gorbachev's common European home from the Urals to the Atlantic or, as the minister has now said, from Vancouver to Vladivostok.
I think this is the way we need to be thinking about the future of security arrangements in Europe. I hope that this is what the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have in mind and had in mind yesterday when they were reputed to be trying to find a way to satisfy the Soviet Union's security concerns vis-a-vis a Germany in NATO. That can only happen if the NATO we are talking about is fundamentally different in its military and political posture than it is now.
One of the ways in which that posture could be changed significantly would be to accept the recommendations that I have just made with respect to short range nuclear weapons and with respect to forward defence, recommendations which are not out of sync with what the minister appears to be thinking himself. I would hope that at some point the government would be able to make that kind of decision.
The Soviet Union's security concerns are deeply rooted in the psyche in the Soviet people. One of the things that I think struck all members of the External Affairs Committee-and I heard the Prime Minister refer yesterday in his speech to the way it affected him-was when we visited a cemetery in Leningrad where 600,000 people are buried, just in one cemetery. This is only a fraction of the people who were killed in the siege of Leningrad and these people are buried in mass graves of 50 to a grave.
One of the first things the young couples who have just been married in the Soviet Union do is to come to the monument and place flowers. That is not something you notice Canadian couples doing at the cenotaphs across the nation. One can pick up how rooted in the whole Soviet consciousness is the reality of war and the fear of war. I take them seriously when they say they do not
Supply
want war because I think they know a lot about it. It is not something that we always appreciate here in Canada.
I just have one final comment on this whole NATO issue. We are now looking for a win-win situation in Europe. We do not want a situation in which there is an expanded NATO that keeps its aggressive political and military posture. We do not want an eastern and central Europe that is in a political security vacuum, so to speak, or incorporated in some way into the western community, with an isolated Soviet Union feeling that it has lost its buffer zone between the Soviet Union and Europe. That would result in a situation in which the Soviets lose not only what they won in the war, but become isolated politically, militarily and economically in the sense that the economic reforms are very difficult and will continue to be very difficult. They will be even more difficult if the west, particularly Europe, takes the wrong attitude toward the Soviet Union and simply says that now that there is a united Germany and Czechoslovakia, Hungary, and everybody is coming back into fold, to hell with the Soviets, let them stew in their own juices.
This is an attitude which we noted some people had when we were in Europe. It is a very dangerous attitude to say that we should let a country which has tens of thousands of nuclear weapons stew in its own juices. I do not want to see a country with that kind of military hardware in chaos, whether that chaos is provoked by economic adversity, ethnic rivalry or whatever the case may be. I do not think that would be in anyone's interest.
On the other hand, I think we need to see some of the events in the Soviet Union in a more positive way than they are sometimes portrayed in the media. For instance, just the other day when Boris Yeltsin was elected as head of the Russian Federation the news said that Mr. Gorbachev's "enemy" had been elected. This is Mr. Gorbachev's political opponent. If we are going to accept that we increasingly have democractization and political pluralism in the Soviet Union, we need to begin to speak of political events in the Soviet Union in a way that is much more comparable to the way we speak of events here, and not overly dramatize the fact that people in the Soviet Union do not agree with each other. In case anybody has not noticed, Canadians have not had a particularly great time agreeing with each other either in

Supply
the last little while. So again, there is a need to change the way we perceive events in the Soviet Union.
I would like to say a word about the Arctic. We were all concerned to hear when we were there that nuclear testing was being shifted from Kazakhstan to a place called, I think, Severnaya Zemlya in the Arctic. We were even more disturbed to learn, after having looked into it, that tests have gone on there before, for something like 15 years until 1963, and most of them atmospheric tests.
This raises the whole question of a comprehensive test ban and the need for Canada to get much more on board than it has been with the nations of the world that are trying to get a conference together through the auspices of the partial test ban treaty to get a comprehensive test ban treaty. Without that, people will be testing to the north of us and testing to the south of us. We will be party to the accumulation of radioactivity on the planet for no good reason, as far as I am concerned,
I would urge the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs to use this new knowledge of what is going on in the Arctic to urge the Americans as well as the Soviets, because the Americans did not respond to the Soviet moratorium on testing when it was in place, to reconsider their views with respect to testing.
Also, naval arms control is an element of the arms race which so far has been neglected. It has not been completely left out of speeches but it has been neglected as far as any real political and international effort is concerned. I met with someone from Greenpeace just yesterday and I know that this is going to become more and more a focus of the peace movement in Canada, and rightfully so. I think that the minister can properly respond to this by using every opportunity that he gets to get naval arms control on to the arms control agenda. If we succeed in doing everything else and have the ocean teeming with submarines which are hard to verify and hard to detect but full of multiple nuclear warheads, we have not exactly increased the safety of the planet.
I see you making funny movements, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The funny movement is that your time has more than expired. I will have to ask for unanimous consent to allow the hon. member extra time. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

I will just wrap things up, and you know how quickly I wrap things up, Mr. Speaker, right to the point.
The question of the peace dividend has been addressed by many people. We have to seize the opportunity in Europe and elsewhere to turn this new era for international co-operation and common security into a way of diverting massive resources which have been consumed for decades now in the building up of arms to the cause of saving the environment and to the cause of bringing the Third World out of the debt ridden and other negative economic circumstances in which it finds itself.
We need to liberate those resources which have so far been captive to the arms race, not because it is a luxury, to use the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but because it is a necessity. It is the only way that, as the human community, we are going to climb out of this hole that we have dug ourselves into over the last 40 years through the arms race, through environmental degradation, and through a global economic system that continues to disadvantage the Third World. We can either climb out of this hole or it can become our grave.
Governments, and particularly Secretaries of State for External Affairs, have tremendous responsibilities, but Canadian Secretaries of State for External Affairs have even more responsibility. Because of the reputation that Canada has in the world and because of the stature we have, we need not to just be peacekeepers, but peacemakers in the final analysis.
I think this new time in which we find ourself in history is an opportunity for Canada to really break out of the mould we have been in, to seize some elements of our tradition that are worthy in terms of external affairs, and to really get about the business of saying the things that need to be said about the way the world has to be changed and of helping those things to happen to the fullest extent possible. If that means being at odds with our friends or with anyone else in the world, then so be it, that is something we do for the sake of the future.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will make three very brief comments if I might. First, on the comprehensive test ban, I agree with the aspirations of the hon. member. Our disagreement with respect to the conference is whether or not that conference would be productive or counterproductive. But despite our reservation about that, we will be present at the conference and our representatives, and our ambassador will be there with
May 31, 1990

instructions to do everything Canada can to make it constructive.
Second, I want to assure the member and the House that not only is the government considering the evolution of SNF policy to which I referred, but so is NATO as a whole. It was discussed at the recent meetings at Kananaskis in Canada. It was discussed at the meetings my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, attended in Brussels last week and it will be on the agenda in Turnberry, Scotland, for a NATO meeting on Wednesday of next week.
We will take part in those discussions, not by removing Canada from the alliance consensus, but rather by trying to shape and affect that alliance consensus. I repeat that I understand precisely what the hon. member is saying about Soviet attitudes. He said it eloquently and effectively. They need to have proof that the changes we are talking about in NATO are happening in fact. I think an opportunity for that to occur is the summit of NATO leaders that has been scheduled for early July in London. Certainly, the Prime Minister and our government are looking to that summit to try to give evidence of some of those kinds of changes.
Finally, on the question of the future of NATO, we believe very strongly and we talk deliberately about the two institutions being complementary. We think that NATO will be necessary and important for as far ahead as we can see. I do not want to get into discussions with a theologian about what is enduring and what is not. I would be interested and look forward to the opportunity to carry on discussions with the hon. member about that issue.
The point I would make is that obviously institutions can force and shape events, but it is very important that institutions not get so far ahead of events that they lose their effectiveness or that actions which are taken designed to be constructive have the opposite effect.

Mr. Speaker, just to expand on the point I was trying to make about NATO's behaviour and posture, I think the minister in his remarks reflected that for the longest time we were wondering in the west whether
Supply
the changes in the Soviet Union were real. I think everyone has come to accept that they are real. I think that the Soviet Union is in a similar position, only they are not quite at the point where they can believe that the changes in the attitude of the west toward them is real. I am suggesting to the minister ways in which we can convince them of this.
The minister uses the familiar argument that Canada wants to shape policy, et cetera, and not act on its own. The point that I would make in return is, why can the government not at least go so far as to say that it thinks that the testing and deployment of these particular weapons would be wrong and it is the Canadian goal to persuade our NATO partners that it is. Other NATO countries have done this over the years. They have taken positions. They may not win the argument, but they have made it clear to their own public what their position is. The public is much more ready to understand failure to persuade others than failure to take a position.
I say this with respect to the need for a continuing Canadian role in Europe. I accept the minister's analysis on that in so far as it is a claim that Canada cannot afford not to be related to Europe. I have this concern as a result of the increasing Americanization of Canada's relationships through the OAS, through the free trade agreement, et cetera.
I would like to see Canada maintain a relationship with Europe in order to balance some of the other foreign policy measures that the government itself has taken. But leaving that aside for a minute, continuing Canadian public support for a Canadian role in the new Europe is only going to exist to the extent that the Canadian public feels that that involvement in Europe is different from and goes beyond the old involvement. Right now I am sure that if you took a poll on whether we should take Canadian troops out of Europe and on policies such as those, they would get a lot of support.
If the minister is looking for continued public support for a Canadian role in Europe, he has to demonstrate to the Canadian public that our role is fundamentally different than what it has been up to this point. I do not think he has done that yet.

May 31, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I think that my colleague and friend from the New Democratic Party raised an extremely important point concerning the future role, indeed the very existence, of NATO. If we follow the line of reasoning used by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, it seems obvious to me that NATO existed and had a military rationale when we faced an enemy; if, to use the minister's own terms, the Poles, Czechs, Hungarians and East Germans are now our friends and no longer a threat to us, the fundamental question we must now ask is whether we should continue to pretend or think that the Russians are still our enemies. In light of the Conservative government's initiatives, of the Prime Minister's visit to the Soviet Union, of the signing of 14 agreements, of President Gorbachev's visit here, I think that we should not consider the Soviets to be our enemies.
The basic issue is what NATO's present and future role should be. I know that the members of NATO insist that all alliance members act together in a co-ordinated fashion. The minister's reply to the question and comments of my New Democratic colleague was that the Canadian government did not want to isolate itself from its NATO partners. Again, I think that is a very conservative position. The government should have the courage to stand out and break new ground very clearly. I make these comments in light of Mr. Gorbachev's statements yesterday when he made a stern warning about a unified Germany. President Gorbachev warned the western allies that excessive pressure to bring a reunified Germany into NATO could compromise the new East-West relationship. NATO is certainly a major military and psychological barrier to the new friendly relations between East and West.
I would like the hon. member to say what he thinks the Canadian government's new attitude should be to these new developments in Eastern Europe in particular.

Mr. Speaker, I think in many respects I answered that question throughout the course of my speech. The Canadian position should be one of seizing new opportunities to have an independent policy within
the limits that the government sees for itself in terms of its own policy obviously.
I do not accept the view that it can be a matter of policy never to disagree or never to take an independent position. The government might take independent positions that I do not even agree with, but I do not think it can be a policy not to have an independent position and to always only take the positions that when one takes totally in concert with others and totally behind closed doors, so to speak.
I think the minister has moved in that direction with the speech he gave on Saturday. I hope this is a sign of things to come. In the meantime, he has a problem with the Minister of National Defence, who does not seem to have cottoned on to this way of thinking. I would hope that very soon we will hear the government speaking with one voice and that one voice will be speaking in the new direction of the new thinking of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and not the standard old NATO routine that we still get from the Minister of Defence.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO THE HON. MEMBER FOR OUTREMONT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, today we celebrate World No-Tobacco Day. Tobacco is the leading cause of preventable disease in the world today. The World Health Organization estimates that if present tobacco use trends continue, 150 million children alive today will eventually die of tobacco induced diseases.
The theme of World No-Tobacco Day this year is "Growing Up Without Tobacco". It is essential that our children be protected from the detrimental effects of tobacco on their health. The vast majority of smokers in Canada started smoking in their teens. If we can prevent young people from starting to smoke, then one day we can eliminate tobacco from our society altogether.
The tobacco industry is attempting to encourage smoking by young people by packaging cigarettes in smaller and cheaper "kiddy packs", and most recently by developing a new type of do-it-yourself cigarette that, through a federal tax loophole, is taxed at a lower rate.
I urge the federal government to protect our young people by prohibiting the sale of tobacco to minors and by introducing measures to control vending machines which give children easy access to this deadly drug.
Our children's health and lives are more important than the profits of the tobacco industry.

Mr. Speaker, the World Health Organization has designated May 31 as World Wide Day Without Tobacco. This year WHO is focusing on the threat to the health of children and youth and has chosen "Growing Up Without Tobacco" as the slogan for the day.
A quote from Travel Through the Interior Parts of North America in 1789 is indeed appropriate:
They are seldom or ever found without a pipe in their mouths, a habit which they acquire in their very infancy. I was very much surprised upon going into one of their houses, in which there was a large family, mostly boys, to find that from the youngest up to the father, they all smoked; nay, one of three years old had a pipe in his mouth.
We have come a long way since 1789 in terms of health care and health promotion, but we still battle the health effects of tobacco smoking, even in 1990.
According to a U.S. study,"over 25 per cent of high school seniors, whoever smoked, had their first cigarette by Grade 6, over 57 per cent had their first cigarette by Grade 8 and 94 per cent had their first cigarette by Grade 11".
In 1988, "more than 35,000 Canadians died prematurely from diseases caused by tobacco". I would hope that the No-Tobacco Day will help raise the consciousness of our young people as it is much easier to not start smoking than it is to quit smoking.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the people of Parrsboro and Cumberland County I want to recognize the efforts of the minister for culture, the Minister of Communications, the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Public Works who have arrived at a cost-sharing formula to provide the federal portion of funding for the fossil museum project in Parrsboro, Nova Scotia.
In conjunction with ACOA these three federal departments will provide federal funding to allow the project to proceed which, in turn, will be the foundation of a tourist industry. It will eliminate the need to send our unique fossils to the United States for research and it will provide employment in an area of limited opportunity. In

May 31, 1990
my view, this will be the best investment the federal government ever made.

Mr. Speaker, I am concerned about the Canadian tourism industry and about the effect this government's policies, especially the pending goods and services tax, are having on the industry.
On May 28, in the consumer and corporate affairs committee a representative of the tourism industry of Canada said the industry will be heavily damaged by the implementation of the GST. Prices for hotels, restaurants, entertainment and sporting activities as well as tour packages will be forced up, causing fewer international travellers to choose Canada as a destination and pushing Canadians who want to travel on their holidays into the lower-priced U.S. tourism market.
He also said the industry was estimating a reduction of more than 25,000 tourism related jobs by 1993 because of the GST.
Mr. Speaker, since tourism means so much to the future of Canadian regional economies, like the one I represent in northwest Saskatchewan, I call on the government to scrap immediately the GST and provide the leadership and the support requested by those in this vital and potentially vibrant industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, drawing a line to determine eligibility is always difficult, but in the case of Canadian firefighters the disqualification of those who retired before August 29, 1985, from receiving the Exemplary Service Medal seems particularly unfair.
Creation of this medal was highly appropriate yet efforts to "grandfather" those who retired before 1985 has so far met no positive response from Government House. As a result some firefighters refuse to wear their medals, others have even returned theirs.
For this reason I have just tabled a motion, seconded by 20 other Progressive Conservative MPs and supported
by many more, seeking the opinion of this House that the Governor General amend the regulations so firefighters with exemplary service who retired before 1985 may also be awarded such decorations.

Mr. Speaker, congratulations are in order for Bell Northern Research. BNR recently completed a $30 million optoelectronics laboratory. This is one of the most advanced in the world and largest in Canada.
Construction of a $100 million laboratory expansion at Bell Northern Research's world headquarters in Nepean begins this summer. The facility will bring together some 4,400 BNR staff and will create a critical mass of research and development expertise unparalleled in the corporation's history.
BNR is already the world leader in several different areas, including the design and development of advanced telecommunications systems, microelectronics, photonics, digital systems and software. Four of the main product lines of the parent company, Northern Telecom, are number one world-wide and others are rising fast.
I am proud to say that BNR is located in Nepean and I am sure all Canadians are doubly proud of BNR's commitment to continued global product leadership through cost-efficient, market-focused research and development.

Mr. Speaker, on May 28, the Prime Minister signed, on behalf of the Government of Canada, the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child in the presence of the UN Secretary General.
This convention was adopted by the UN General Assembly on November 20, 1989 after 10 years of preparation. It represents major progress in the protection of children's rights since it contains a number of general essential provisions which guarantee that their basic needs and interests will be addressed. It also
May 31, 1990

provides for the protection of children in particularly difficult circumstances.
By signing the convention after actively participating in its development, Canada is confirming its support for this global cause.
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Prime Minister of Canada as well as the provinces and territories for supporting the ratification of this Convention by Canada.

Mr. Speaker, residents of Canada's smallest province would like to add their voices to those of the 72 per cent of Canadians who oppose this government's high interest rate policy.
Even at the best of times when interest rates are low, the Prince Edward Island economy is not all that strong and annual growth is unsteady. If you take away a major employer, like CFB Summerside, the economy really gets hurt. Add high interest rates and the situation could very well become critical. Farmers, fishermen, small business people and all Islanders, in one way or another, are affected by the hefty increase in the price of money which this government has allowed to take place.
I urge the government, on behalf of all Islanders who oppose this high interest rate policy, to see the financial and human toll its actions are taking and to finally act in this country's national interest.

Mr. Speaker, today is World No-Tobacco Day, a day organized by the World Health Organization to promote the idea of a world free from tobacco use.
Canada has been exceptionally active in instituting and implementing a national strategy to reduce tobacco use. As a result of this program, which includes increased taxes and implementation of two significant pieces of legislation, the Tobacco Products Control Act and the Non-Smokers' Health Act, tobacco consumption in
Canada has declined by 6.8 per cent in 1989 and by over 20 per cent during the first third of 1990.
The former Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Hon. Jake Epp, is to be awarded the Award of Excellence for exceptional leadership in creating a tobacco-free Canada by the Canadian Council on Smoking and Health.
On World No-Tobacco Day, Canada can rightfully claim its place as a world leader in the control of tobacco use.

Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed in the member for Portage-Interlake. He condemned the Core Area Initiatives Programs without really knowing a great deal about them. If he had stopped to study them, he would realize that there are programs there to improve the educational and career aspects of natives, multicultural and multiracial groups, young children, senior and elementary students with literacy problems. These programs will be cut unless this initiative is renewed. This is going to be cut during the International Year of Literacy which I find completely appalling.

How very hypocritical, cutting programs this year! And the attack against the weakest and most destitute Canadians goes on. These programs should be re-instated immediately.

Mr. Speaker, the corporate welfare bum of the week features this week a two-time nominee, Alcan Aluminum Limited. Alcan paid only $39 million in federal taxes in 1987 after profits of $433 million and received a $6 million tax credit on $270 million in profits in 1986.
The second nominee is Goodyear Canada which got a tax credit of $1.4 million on $11 million in 1988.
The third nominee is Fletcher Challenge Finance which paid no tax in 1988 on profits of $24 million.

May 31, 1990
Oral Questions
Now, for the winner. The envelope, please. And the winner is Alcan Aluminum. Alcan chief executive officer, David Culver, who led the corporate sector to fight for the free trade deal, made $1.4 million in 1988. Alcan found plenty of money to get the trade deal and to pay Mr. Culver, but not to pay its fair share of federal taxes. This makes Alcan the corporate welfare bum of the week.

Mr. Speaker, according to the latest Gallup poll, 54 per cent of Canadians are willing to pay a $100 income tax surcharge to help protect the environment.
This is good news for it indicates that there is a high level of public concern. The bad news is that the government might try to exploit the public's concern by levying an unnecessary green tax.
If the government had considered the environment in the tax reform process, there would be no need even to contemplate an environmental surcharge. Instead of the regressive GST, Canada should have a progressive tax system to encourage green consumption and production and to cut pollution.
It is not easy to be green, but so far the government has not even tried. When will the Minister of Finance see the green light?

Mr. Speaker, the statements made recently by the member for Saint-Maurice regarding the premier and the people of Newfoundland were unfortunate. I will not repeat the words here. It would serve no useful purpose.
Indeed, there is no place for that kind of language in a great national debate. The words were spoken with emotion and with anger. I want to say that the member for Saint-Maurice has demonstrated today the courage and decency required to apologize to the premier and the people of Newfoundland for those remarks.
I have known the member as a colleague on the transport committee for six years. I know the remarks he
made were out of character for him, and I accept his apology.
With the national debate that will be ongoing in the days ahead, it is understanding and sensitivity that we must demonstrate for each other and to each other, not emotion and anger.
I hope the quick apology by the member for Saint-Maurice and the quickly accepted apology by the premier and I believe the people of Newfoundland for those words are an example to the nation and in particular the first ministers as they begin their important deliberations this weekend and in the days ahead.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
Today, the Minister of National Revenue unveiled a totally new proposal for collecting the GST from certain small businesses. In doing so the minister in effect admitted that the government's original proposal was an administrative nightmare for small business. In fact it was totally unworkable, but this proposal today does not really change any of that.
Under this plan the government wants to collect GST of up to 1.75 per cent from some grocery and convenience stores on all their sales. How can the government continue to say it is not taxing food when it wants to collect from some grocery and convenience stores a flat rate GST on all their sales including basic groceries?
