We worked very hard to bring together figures and data to make sure we can help 800,000 small businesses to work in a better way with the GST. I think it
May 31, 1990

is good news for small businesses. We have consulted those businesses and they are onside with us.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again the minister has failed to even mention the Canadian consumer.

The proposal of the Minister of National Revenue today will not make the GST any easier for Canadians generally. They will still have to pay 7 per cent more on just about everything they buy.
What is worse is that businesses opting for the new scheme are being told by the Minister of National Revenue that they will not have to show the GST on their sales receipts or anywhere.
What happened to the government's commitment to visibility? Why is the government even ceasing to try to have the tax visible? Why is the government proposing a band-aid solution for an unfair tax that even major surgery cannot save? Why will the government not scrap this tax and go back to the drawing-board?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for External Affairs. Yesterday, President Gorbachev warned the Western Allies that excessive pressure to have a reunified Germany join NATO could seriously jeopardize the new East-West relations. Genscher and Mitterand have both drawn different scenarios.
Could the minister tell the House what he thinks of them and whether he is now convinced of the need to develop a new compromise which is not exactly what the West has been proposing since the discussions started concerning a reunified Germany?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there is no question that there is very evident concern on the part of the Soviet Union, the people and the Government of the Soviet Union, with regard to some of the external implications of the unification of Germany.
As the Prime Minister said yesterday in his remarks at the luncheon with Mr. Gorbachev, it is important that those sensitivities be understood and be responded to.
It is our considered view, that an important step toward resolving that question would be for NATO to take actions that demonstrated that the reform in NATO that we have been talking about is in fact being achieved. That path is being pursued and was pursued by colleague the Minister of National Defence and his colleagues during recent meetings both in Kananaskis in Canada and in Brussels. They were discussed yesterday by Mr. Gorbachev and the Prime Minister. They were discussed today in the debate provoked by the hon. member's motion.
We believe that those kind of actions, if they are reflected in the summit meeting on NATO in early July in London, can make it more possible for the concerns of the Soviet Union, which we understand, to be met.

Does this mean that the Canadian government asked the Soviets to lift the economic blockade which, as we know, was decreed over a month ago? Might the President have rejected this suggestion?

That was a comment made in the context of the discussion of Lithuania.
I raised with Mr. Shevardnadze the question as to whether or not there was a blockade particularly of medical supplies. He said he thought there was no blockade but he gave me the understanding that if Canadians wanted to send medical supplies to any hospital anywhere in the Soviet Union, including in Lithuania, there would be no unusual obstacles put in the path.
He went on to say, and I appreciated it particularly, that if other concerns of this kind regarding commodities other than medical supplies arose that he thought the quickest way to deal with them would be for himself and myself to establish an arrangement by which I would

While I do not want to underestimate the divergences on the remaining issues, what is in dispute is modest when compared with what is really at stake.
What is really at stake is Canada.

Failure would compromise our capacity for living together in unity and diminish our capacity to maintain the kinds of prosperity that Canadians have enjoyed over so many decades. It would waste an opportunity to close a chapter in our constitutional history with the full partnership of all the provinces in our Confederation, including the assent of those provinces who were partners when Confederation began.
It would curtail opportunities for constitutional change, in such important areas as Senate reform and aboriginal rights, for the foreseeable future. I believe it would send a very damaging signal about Canada to the international community with consequences for our national well-being.

Ratification of the accord, on the other hand, would mean that we could turn the page of constitutional reform and get on with other unfinished business also of great importance to Canadians.
It would allow us to build together on a solid foundation of national unity.

It would send a signal of stability to the international community, ending the consternation in many parts of the world about what is going on in Canada. It would end the puzzlement why anyone in such a respected nation would fail to appreciate the value of its strength and prosperity to the world community. People across the world are genuinely troubled about why anyone would fail to understand the magnificence of this great country, Canada.
Elsewhere, political repression, poverty, famine, natural disasters, not arcane constitutional debates are the stuff of national turmoil. Canadians are looking to their First Ministers for leadership and action now.
May 31, 1990



Elsewhere, as I was just saying, political repression, poverty, famine and natural disasters, not arcane constitutional debates, however important, are the stuff of national turmoil.
Canadians are looking to their First Ministers for leadership and action now.
Canadians are looking not for fine words but for common sense and responsibility.

Canadians are looking not for constitutional niceties but for common sense and responsibility. As Premier Ghiz, leader of Canada's smallest province said: "Canadians are saying, 'Save Canada. Make it work'." I believe when Premier Ghiz said: "Save Canada. Make it work," he was speaking for millions of Canadians who want Canada to make it work.
If there is the political will to break the impasse, surely there is a constitutional way. I am inviting First Ministers to a working dinner on Sunday evening to find out if sufficient political will truly exists. If our discussions go well, we will continue at a First Ministers' Conference to begin the next morning. Our dinner will take place on June 3, three years to the day, I believe, when I, along with 10 premiers representing four different political parties, signed the Meech Lake Accord. That same accord was overwhelmingly endorsed by all three parties in the House of Commons on two different occasions.
I give Canadians my commitment, and I know I speak on behalf of all members of the House of Commons, to make every effort to produce an agreement. Once we have that agreement I give my commitment to Canadians to persevere on outstanding constitutional issues such as Senate reform and aboriginal rights, so important to so many Canadians across the country.
This country will not realize its unparalleled promise until all Canadians believe that their Constitution affirms their rights and reflects their values. That is why Quebec's voluntary endorsement of the existing constitution will make it a vibrant document of unity and hope for Canada and the future.
Routine Proceedings

It is a golden opportunity! Since Quebec has affirmed its faith in a united Canada, it is a golden opportunity for Canada to find in its heart and soul the ability to say yes to Quebec; it is time to build a completely unified country once and for all.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, we have inherited a great land built on the tolerance, vision and labour of generations of Canadians before us. Many of the members on all sides of this House of Commons are sons and daughters of immigrants. When the Leader of the Opposition rose in this House on another occasion he made a most moving address about his own personal experience. I thought as I listened to him that day a few months ago what a magnificent and splendid country this is, where in all parts of this country and all parts of this House, in one generation alone, the children of immigrants have risen to positions of great authority, making it clear to all the world that this is truly, in the very best sense of the word, a civilization that represents the fundamentals of a genuine democracy.
Hear, hear.

And so we have inherited a very great land, a truly great land, all of us in this House of Commons, members from British Columbia to Newfoundland and Labrador. It is now our responsibility to turn Canada over to our children and eventually our grandchildren undamaged and undiminished, and to bequeath them a nation that stands proudly united before history and before all humanity as one of the world's privileged lands, blessed as it always has been, our Canada, by the hand of God.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we of the Official Opposition have been calling for a First Ministers' Conference as a way of breaking and finding a solution to the constitutional impasse for some time.
It has been our belief that it should have been called by the Prime Minister before now and that he should not have waited until today to call a First Ministers' Conference.

May 31, 1990
Routine Proceedings
I know that the Prime Minister has been concerned about the risk if there is such a meeting and it is not a success. But, Mr. Speaker, there are also risks, perhaps even greater risks, if such a meeting is not held at all.
The provincial premiers themselves have been calling for such a meeting for some days now, perhaps the strongest argument why the Prime Minister should not have waited until today to make his announcement.
The Prime Minister today said that he is "inviting First Ministers to a working dinner on Sunday evening to find out if sufficient political will truly exists". He went on to say: "If our discussions go well, we will continue at a First Ministers' Conference to begin the next morning."
Mr. Speaker, this is certainly a step in the right direction and a step that we welcome. It is, in a sense, more than simply a step, because for the first time since Premier McKenna proposed a companion resolution, the Prime Minister is agreeing that there should be a dialogue involving the Prime Minister and all the provincial premiers around the same table. This kind of dialogue involving all the First Ministers and giving all of them an equal opportunity to discuss this matter, a matter crucial for the future of our country, is what has been missing until now.
I must say that I have some concern that there is a firm commitment from the Prime Minister so far only to a working dinner. I think Canadians would have got more reassurance from his announcement and would have preferred if it was a firm commitment for a First Ministers' Conference as well.
There are important questions to deal with: Senate reform, aboriginal rights, the rights of language minorities, the rights of multicultural groups and others.

Mr. Speaker, we co-operated with government members on the Charest Committee because the Liberals wanted to resolve the constitutional deadlock, and it is our earnest wish that the discussions with the Premiers will be a success, a success that will benefit all of Canada.

We want to see steps as a result of the discussions announced today, and Canadians want to see steps as a result of these discussions that will confirm the future of our country.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians generally should recognize, and I think most of them do, that the success we have had as a country is substantial compared to most of the other countries of the world. Canadians generally want this success to continue and to increase.

Mr. Speaker, we want this success to extend to these discussions, for the future of our country and all Canadians.

We are concerned about the future of our country. We must work together to ensure it continues strong and prosperous for ourselves and future generations.

Mr. Speaker, we, too, welcome the announcement by the Prime Minister that there be a meeting of First Ministers. I think that this is the time to set aside our normal partisan concerns and wish all the First Ministers well when they meet here Sunday.
Hear, hear!

We hope that the accord does not die quietly at the dinner table and, if there is a new deal, that the Prime Minister will inform and involve the Canadian people in as much and as reasonable a way as possible throughout the process.
The issue at stake is the unity of this country and the winner, in the end, must be Canada. This could be the most important meeting that the First Ministers of this country have ever held in their 123 year history of Canada and we must set aside partisan concerns to make sure there is an agreement.
I suppose I only have two messages at this time, Mr. Speaker. One is to the premiers. I realize the premiers are premiers of their own provinces from different parts of this country but all premiers must never forget that first and foremost they are Canadians and the interests of Canada must come first.
May 31, 1990

Second, I say to the Prime Minister of Canada that the Prime Minister must be the Prime Minister. He must be the one who leads and speaks out for all of Canada. The Prime Minister must be the one, on behalf of all of us, who rises to the occasion to find the accommodation.

Mr. Speaker, to Quebecers it is important that the rest of Canada accents Quebec as part of Canada, while acknowledging that Quebec is different and that it has a special place within our country as a distinct society.
Mr. Speaker, it is now time to put the interests of our countiy ahead of the interests of the parties in this House.

Finally, in addition to the five important proposals from Quebec that all parties in the House endorse and have endorsed on more than one occasion, it is also important, as the Prime Minister said, that we address the other concerns of equally tremendous importance. The concerns of aboriginal rights, the concerns of the multiracial people and those of multicultural background in the country, the concerns of northern Canadians to make them a full partner within Canada and the concern in many parts of the country for real and genuine reform of the other place, the Senate, must also be addressed. As well, we must address the concern of having constitutional change evolve in a really democratic and open process. Many people complained in the past that that was not there.
There are many other concerns to address such as the ongoing concerns of minority groups and women in the country. I, along with everybody else in the country, hope for success on the weekend. We welcome the fact that there will be a First Ministers' meeting, and we hope that, when the agreement comes-I say when it comes, and I am sure it will come-it will be an agreement that will unite Canadians, bind them together and make us proud of our Constitution and country.

I wish the federal and provincial First Ministers good luck!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while every member of this House is likely focused on the great debate going on inside our boundaries about questions that both unify us and divide us, there is a big world out there which is also going through its own volatility and incredible forces of change and development.

Like all other members of this House, I hope that we will have a meeting next Sunday to unify the country and especially to consider the interests of all the regions and to find a way to solve the problems in the country.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, we have a very important opportunity to establish a new international role.

The purpose of the very important proposal put forward by my colleague, the member for Papineau, is to bring to the attention of this House many of those issues. The world impinges upon Canada, perhaps to a far greater degree than ever before in our history. The real test is how do we respond. What is our answer? What direction do we take and what kind of-to use an
over-worked word-vision do we have about the role we will play in this rapidly changing world where the earthquake of revolution takes place every single day of the week.
I would like to stop for a moment to share an experience that some members of the committee had when we were travelling in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union a few short weeks ago.
We had the privilege of being in Berlin on May Day, a remarkable day. The wall had come down and thousands of people were walking back and forth. During the course of conversation a young woman who was our translator was talking about the incredible change that had gone on three or four months ago when the secret police and the police dogs had been guarding the boundaries. All of a sudden there was a Woodstock atmosphere where there was beer, sausages, and rock bands playing on the streets.
This young woman who had been a participant and was an active member of the crowd that gathered around the church last November 9, which was the spark that brought down the dictatorship in East Germany, said something very important that I do not think I will ever forget. In talking to her about what she would be doing, and she knew we were politicians from Canada, she said: "Please don't take away from us what we won at the church that day. Don't usurp the kind of achievement and the change that we want to bring about".
What she was talking about was the end of military alliances, the end the confrontation, the end of conventional cold war thinking and actions which have so dominated this world for the past 40 years. It was interesting to note that that heartfelt cry made by that young woman was repeated the next day by the newly appointed Minister of State for Foreign Affairs in the East German Government, a young man by my standards. He said that it was time to get rid of the old, conventional ways of thinking. He saw the unification of Germany as a way of breaking out of the Warsaw-NATO kind of confrontation that had been around for so long. He said: "We must apply our energy and our thoughts to what is new. How do we bring about a new synthesis in Europe to respond to this?"
When I was watching the news last night I was thinking about the faces of the people of Ottawa gathering
May 31, 1990

around Mr. Gorbachev as he walked up and down the streets. In effect the people of this city, perhaps on behalf of all Canadians, were saying the same kind of thing. There was hope in those faces. They were not simply attracted to Mr. Gorbachev because he is a celebrity. I think they also saw him as a symbol of real change. They saw him as someone who in his own right and in his own country, had initiated an incredible revolution of thought and action. They were reaching out with those hands, not just to the man but to what he represented.
The debate that we have to focus on today concerns how we can ensure that those hopes and expectations of that young woman in East Berlin and of the people of Ottawa are not usurped, not taken away. The response of the politicians, the diplomats, the officials, the bureaucrats, and the people in power with authority must be to understand that kind of undercurrent, that strong willingness of hope and expectation is running around and is oftentimes in danger of being kidnapped by those who have vested interests in keeping things the way they are.
The contrast to that reaching out of the people on the streets of Ottawa was the results of what we saw in the discussions between our leaders and those of the Soviets which once again was in cold war language. Our people say: "We want NATO". Mr. Gorbachev says: "We cannot get into NATO". All of a sudden we were pulling back, were retreating from the impulse and incredible momentum that had been started on the streets of eastern Europe, aided and abetted by policies. I think of the progress that has been made in reducing arms and looking toward new accommodations which is in danger of regressing. It is in danger of being pulled back by those who have power and authority.
I address these remarks to the members of this House because I think we all share the hope that that will not take place but understand the threat that is there.
I want to address for a moment the question put forward in my colleague's motion about the incoherence and the sense of confusion that sometimes exist in our own government. I do not blame a government for being caught unawares by these changes. Goodness gracious, no one pretends that they have omniscient wisdom about
Supply
what was going to take place, but I think we can honestly say that we expect a little more than what we received.
On the one hand, we had the Minister of National Defence as part of a NATO meeting out in Alberta a couple of weeks ago endorsing the concept of maintaining nuclear weapons in NATO and saying that that is the way it is going to be. On the other hand, last Saturday night the Secretary of State for External Affairs was saying: "Maybe we shouldn't do that". Who do we believe? Which minister is speaking for the government? It is hard to determine.
When questions were asked in the House by the member for Papineau-Saint-Michel, the House Leader and others, we could not get a clear answer. They did not seem to know who was speaking for the country.
That is not uncommon, but this is too critical a situation in which to play the normal kind of political games. Surely, it is up to members on this side of the House, and I would say to members of the Conservative caucus, to say: "That's not good enough. That doesn't meet the expectations of the millions of people around this country who want something different".
I point out to you as well, Mr. Speaker, the other kinds of issues that have emerged recently. Look at the opportunity that we have had as a country to start building some bridges. What is clear in the debate so far, the debate we have heard in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, is that we cannot presume that we can maintain our way of doing things, our structures, our alliances and say to the Soviet Union: "Sorry, you lost the game". This is not some kind of football match where there are winners and losers. We have to find a way of some common interest.
I suppose one thing that is most vivid in my memory of my trip to the Soviet Union is how deep tire feeling is about the impact of the Second World War and the deep need for security. Part of the whole movement in eastern Europe for the past 40 years has been how to defend themselves against a reoccurrence of the Second World War. For a moment we have to put ourselves in the shoes of the Soviets to say: "How do they gain that security when they see a unified Germany joining NATO with the presence of nuclear weapons on their soil? How can we give them a sense that it is not happening all over again?" I know it may be irrational and emotional, but the fact of the matter is that it is real. It is not good

May 31, 1990
Supply
enough for our leaders to say: "Sorry, that is the way it is going to be".
We are making a plea, as the member for Papineau- Saint-Michel said this morning, to look at this thing in a new light, to have a sense of new understanding of what is going on.
There is a need for a new architecture of political structures around the world, but particularly in eastern Europe. I take at face value Mr. Gorbachev's proposal that he wants a home that stretches from the Soviet Union right to North America. It is clear that we need structure to make that happen and it is not in place.
I accept with some credit the proposals put forward by the government that perhaps NATO can only be a transition phase. That is good, but let us go one step beyond and say that it will be a transition to something that will represent a larger scale collective security organization covering the Soviet Union, eastern and western Europe, and North America, where we share collective security and not where we are divided by it. I think that is the statement that the Soviets are waiting to hear from western leaders. We must add our voice in our own councils of the NATO Alliances, the OECDs, the summit meetings, and so on.
Canadians have a particular opportunity, not that we are going to be the major players. When we start to look at how to put the building blocks of that new structure together there are ways of doing it. We have seen it in front of us.
Surely, one of the most critical areas of concern that we share with the Soviets, the Americans, and many European countries is our Arctic. In 1987 President Gorbachev issued the Murmansk declaration stating that we should have some kind of treaty for the Arctic. When we were in the Soviet Union we had a response from people saying that we could have that. Members of the Arctic Institute in Leningrad said that there should be a denuclearized treaty for the Arctic. There is some common ground to build upon.
However, Mr. Gorbachev has come and gone from Ottawa with no mention of that proposal. No significant steps were taken toward negotiations or discussions on that very significant initiative.

speechtext: What did they discuss?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Well, that is part of the problem.
We know that Ottawa is famous for its hospitality and its restful, calm, tranquil atmosphere. It is a wonderful place to get rid of jet lag, but when you have the President of the Soviet Union here you expect more than a good night's rest.
I would say that here was an opportunity to demonstrate our interest and willingness to build some bridges, to put together new building blocks that would have helped on the security issue and one that would have helped us. I am not talking about being altruistic with the Soviets. Goodness knows that our security interests are directly in the Arctic. That is where U.S. and Russian submarines are playing tag all the time and where we need some kind of arrangement.
I see by today's The Financial Post that my view is shared by Allan Fotheringham who says that great minds think alike.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
I say that with tongue in cheek, Mr. Speaker.
The fact of the matter is that we have a real interest in developing these building blocks. In the area of the economy there is an enormous opportunity to develop a whole set of relationships in the Soviet Union, a country desperate for transfers of technology, trade, and investment. The expectations of that country were raised during the last prime ministerial visit by the signing of a number of agreements. Almost a year later, nothing has been done. We have not lived up to those agreements.
Some of the problems are those of the Soviets and many of the problems are our own. The fact of the matter is that we can say without any contradiction that our ability to meet the demands emerging in the Soviet for building a new set of relationships is not being met.
I will tell you one of the reasons why. Let us just take a look at one simple statistic. The Department of External Affairs has 30 posts in western Europe, but just six in eastern Europe, including the Soviet Union. How do we expect to begin to manage a whole new set of relationships, economically, culturally and politically, when we are totally understaffed, under-resourced and do not have the capacity to do it? Claims may be made for budget or restraint reasons, but how can we argue for budget reasons that we are maintaining a corporal's guard in the fastest changing, most dynamic area in the world when everyday we are losing all kinds of opportunities?
May 31, 1990

Let me give one example. I was sitting at a Kiwanis club dinner a week ago with the president of a lumber firm in Manitoba who talked about trying to negotiate a lumber agreement between the Soviets and Canada. They would use a barter system to bring certain kinds of wood into Canada that are not available here. We know in western Canada that we have to start purchasing more from the Soviets in order to maintain the balance because of our grain trade where we have by far the greatest surplus on the trade side.
As he said that getting somebody to help him to work through the red tape and to get the front-end logistics in place was just not possible. He has given up. It is a small example, but I am sure members in this House can repeat the example a hundredfold from their own ridings. We are simply not equipped to meet the demand. We are simply not there in the numbers or in the capacity that we need to respond to those kinds of changes.
I would like to point out another area where we are not providing the leadership in that building block. We have heard in the House today and in the last couple of weeks about the growing problem dealing with nuclear energy. In our country, the Soviet Union, and eastern Europe peaceful uses of nuclear energy is one of the most important areas of common concern.
What would happen if we proposed that there be a common agency which would look after standards, investment, safety and health problems between the Soviet Union and Canada? In part, we would help them with the enormous clean-up problems they have with Chernobyl. We would deal with the problems of the Candu in Romania. We could all of a sudden, I am sure, find some common ground. We could find an area where we can share common interests. It would be the kind of agency that would give us a working relationship in a new area but one vital to our economies and our inter-relationships. We could establish once again a new kind of foundation, putting another block in place that would lead to the new structures and architecture that would bring together the east, the west, and North America.
I think back to when I was still going to university. I read about the theory of Jean Monet in starting the European Common Market. He said that it should be started with functional agencies and then you build from functional agencies into some kind of political agencies to the point where they now have the European Common Market. They started that way. They had the steel
Supply
authority. Then they started working on transportation and coal. The thesis was that this was a way to get to know one another, to establish some common lines of communication and interest. From that you start to build up the super-structure.
Are we not in a similar condition today? Are we not as Canadians, in a position to take those initiatives where there is such a direct and close common interest between the two?
That is what I think the member for Papineau-Saint-Michel means in his motion when he says that we need a coherent policy. We need some direction. We need some creative thinking in this area.
In particular, we need it in terms of our own domestic opportunities. One of the great assets we have as Canadians is that we have a population built upon many Canadians whose origins are in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. I think of my own city of Winnipeg where we have a Ukrainian Canadian community of great strength and vitality, as well as Poles and Russians and Germans and all the rest. They understand the culture and the language and have relatives in their home land. There is an enormous sort of criss-cross of connections, people who are anxious at the present moment to go back to the homeland, to go back to where their relatives are to establish commercial or business relationships.
In speaking to many of them they say that they do not know who to talk to, they do not know where to go. Even if the Prime Minister was to designate one member of the cabinet and say: "You are responsible for the Soviet Union. You bring together private business. You bring together the regions. You bring together the cultural groups".
Let us talk about language training in Canada. Let us talk about new transportation links into the Soviet Union. Let us talk about how we get some investment guarantees, whatever it is that will provide some kind of focal point for all those groups to come together. We have this incredible resource in our own country that will give us an enormous sort of outreach into the Soviet Union and eastern Europe and we are not utilizing it.
Many of them are doing it individually, but many are being frustrated because they will arrive in Kiev and all of sudden say: "Who do I talk to?" It is clear to us from our own examination that one cannot find answers immediately in the Soviet Union. There are a lot of complications. Many smaller businesses do not have the front-end capacity to do it. That is where the Government of Canada comes in.

May 31, 1990
Supply
When we spoke to the West Germans about the commercial side they told us that when the Soviets sit down and talk about providing credit of a billion dollars on a big project, the West Germans say that in return they want some understanding that there will be no red tape. They get their business done that way. You need somebody who has got that eye on the sparrow, who knows where they are going with that kind of direction.
We are suggesting in this motion that we have not tapped into that well of Canadian interest, those resources, and have not even drawn upon members of Parliament in terms of an open consultation. The member for Papineau-Saint-Michel said very properly this morning that it is a certain insult to this House that the Secretary of State for External Affairs started to announce a policy when he knows full well that the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade has been working on one for close to a year and he has not had the courtesy to wait a couple of weeks to see what it is going to say.
What is the point? Why have 14 members of Parliament spend almost a year working at this and then rush ahead to the finish line? It is not a competition. We are not in a race with the Secretary of State. We are not out there to win the red ribbon. We want to help. The fact of the matter is that it creates enormous complication by doing that.
What we are trying to condemn the government or tell it to get its act together. It must understand that this is one of the most important moments in our history. If we do not do it right we are going to find ourselves isolated. We are going to find ourselves pushed out of Europe. We are going to find ourselves without the connecting links into the Soviet Union. We will not have the kind of influence that we should have.
Without proper action we will not be able to build upon the assets that we have, which includes a good reputation, a population in Canada that is ready and willing and has the attributes based upon their own culture and language to help. This is simply because we have not focused on the problem. We do not have a policy. We do not have a direction. We are not mobilizing the resources of this House and all the people within it to try to bring together a common front. This is not an issue that necessarily divides us as parties. We are all interested in recognizing this enormous challenge and at the same time the opportunity it represents. We are all
here to help, but it is the government that has the responsibility to provide the ability for that help and that co-operation to be targeted at this very important part of the world.

I would just like to ask my colleague if he could say a little bit about the reaction he received when he was in the Soviet Union concerning Canada's role and how we can be more supportive.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the question.
Their reaction in some cases was puzzlement. There had been an enormous sense of optimism built around the trip last year of the Prime Minister, followed by the Speaker of the House, which I think established a set of relationships and expectations. Agreements were signed. As I say, almost a year later we are waiting for some delivery. There is a feeling of disappointment that many of these kinds of developments have not taken place.
May 31, 1990

I do not say this to be critical, because I think there is a problem on both sides. They are afraid of being caught up in a kind of diplomatic minuet that oftentimes takes place.
As people from the Arctic Institute said, there was an Arctic environmental agreement signed. The scientists were in agreement. But it seems that somehow the officials got in the way and nothing has been done in this crucial area.
Here we have, as we discovered, the prospect of the Soviet Union initiating nuclear tests in the Arctic. This is an area about which there should be a very major outcry. Because there is no commission in place-we have not even appointed the commissioners yet to make it work- the forum has been lost. We have not had the opportunity to create the very essential dialogue that is needed.
I would also like to comment, if I may, on the agricultural area. We were asked, again during the visit of the Prime Minister, and proposals were put on the table, that we help set up a series of model farms in the Soviet Union using Canadian technology, fertilizers and methodologies as a way of demonstrating a new way of productivity in the agricultural area. Land was being offered. The invitation was there. Yet we did not take them up on it. Now the Dutch and the Italians are doing it and we are not in the marketplace. We asked why. They said: "Well, we did not have the resources to bring it together. We did not have the capacity to do it".
Again, I want to express as a western Canadian that when we say we do not have the resources, I must think of the enormous resources we have in my own City of Winnipeg to have brought that kind of thing to fruition. Somehow it fell in a hole. It just did not materialize. It is those kinds of disappointments that are there which I think are creating wonderment as to whether we are really as serious as our statements claim.
I would have to speak of my own personal disappointment with what has transpired in the last 24 hours. I think the occasion of Mr. Gorbachev's visit here was an opportunity to pin some of these things down, to clear away some of the brush, to get away from some of the red tape and to pin-point some of these problems, whether on the Arctic treaty, nuclear testing, or on commercial agreements. Yet we did not seem to come out with very much.
Supply
As I have not seen anything in the papers, I do not even think we got a commitment on a new agreement on wheat, which has been a kind of bedrock of our relationship with the Soviet Union for the last 20 years.
It is those kinds of things that we are concerned about which show a lack of energy, a lack of focus and a lack of direction.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad we are having this thorough airing today of Canadian foreign policy in central and eastern Europe. The hon. member's motion which has brought us into this, is predicated on the allegation that there is a lack of initiative and some confusion. I would like to pick up on that in my remarks and refute it with some of the evidence of what has been going on.
Before getting into that I would like to say that just as this debate is timely, following on the heels of the visit by both Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev and Foreign Minister Eduard Shevardnadze, last Saturday in the Etobicoke-Lakeshore constituency which I represent, we had a one-day policy forum on Canadian policy in central and eastern Europe. It was an opportunity for an exchange of views and information, participated in by well over 400 Canadians, many of whom have been not only to the Soviet Union but in Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and so on, actively engaged in education, in trade, in cultural activities, in business opportunities and so on.
It was there that the Secretary of State for External Affairs made the remarks that he did, outlining some very important new directions in Canadian foreign policy in that area, the burden of which he carried through on in his remarks here this morning to the House.
I would like to elaborate on some of the points which the Secretary of State for External Affairs made in the general framework by giving some specifics. If foreign policy exists, it is not only in general principles and broad terms but it does come to earth in specific applications. That is what I would like to talk about. In so doing I would like to indicate that Canada is moving in a new and uncharted area with some foreign policy successes.

May 31, 1990
Supply
I think that the speech given by the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona, typically for him, was both informed and informing. He took a very thoughtful and balanced approach on this.
I know that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said that we should approach these issues beyond party lines and try to work together. I think that is the important spirit.
I heard the member for Papineau-Saint-Michel talking this morning about a lack of initiatives, yet in the same sentence he mentioned that the Prime Minister had signed a major accord in Moscow last November. The hon. member from Winnipeg said that a year has passed since that was signed, while in fact it is only half a year. I heard the member for Papineau-Saint-Michel talking about a lack of initiative and lamenting that Canada has no consulate in Leningrad and in the same sentence he talked about the opening of a Canadian consulate in Kiev, I really think-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
The fact is that all these initiatives are taking place. Canada is supporting a new and active working relationship with the reformist central and eastern European countries. We are assisting, along with other western countries, in the process of revitalizing this region. It is a very hard task because they themselves have a lot to sort out. They are in transition. I think that anyone who is honest with himself would not be so critical about the Canadian response as to look for it as having no contradictions and as being completely developed even while the situation there is still developing. We should be open, frank, and non-partisan in this area, and recognize that we are in a world of change and that Canada is responding in that area.
At the economic summit in Paris last July, Canada joined with the other nations in the G-7 in supporting the reforms in Poland and Hungary and in pledging to support the transformation of those economies in a durable manner with both economic assistance and other means. This is something on which we have followed through in a positive way.
The opposition asks about initiatives. Here is some Canadian action. We have created a $42 million assistance package for Poland and Hungary. This package
was announced last November and it has three major elements to it.
First, $12 million has been spent in emergency food aid. This food was not just purchased in Canada and taken to Poland. More important, it was sold there and the equivalent of $6 to $8 million in Polish zloty was earned for a jointly-administered counterpart fund that is today funding developments in rural parts of Poland. That is very important.
A second element was the $20 million revolving short-term export credit insurance that was established for Poland. There has been no lack of initiative at all.
A third element is the clear initiative of putting in place $10 million over five years for economic development.
I will give you six or eight examples of Canadian foreign policy success to show what we are doing to help with economic development. Four hundred and fifty thousand dollars has gone to the International Management Centre in Budapest to create the Canada Fund which supports management training. In fact, the dean of that school will be a Canadian. This is beyond the stage of putting money into countries, money which is in short supply here. That, moreover, is not what they need. They need, want, and are seeking from us assistance in such things as management training and restructuring of government. There is one veiy positive example of an initiative in that area.
Second, two contracts with the Canadian Executive Services Overseas are now providing 41 volunteer professionals in both Hungary and Poland who will work as industrial and business consultants. That is another positive initiative along the same theme.
Third, a Canadian company is doing an evaluation study of possible new and upgraded edible oil processing plants in Poland.
A fourth initiative is a $2 million training program for Polish farmers in livestock and farm management. This is really a creative initiative. This summer over 100 Polish farmers will be coming to Canada for intensive courses at a training institute. They will get practical experience on Canadian farms.
A fifth example of an initiative is the $1 million program of support for the Warsaw Agricultural University and three associated institutes involved in training and research for Polish agriculture.
The sixth example in just this one element is the assistance in establishing the English-French Language Training Centre. Its curriculum focuses on language proficiency but also on the principles, in the course of
May 31, 1990

that, of representative government, democratic processes, local administration, and human rights.
I can go on, Mr. Speaker. There are a lot of these initiatives. There is a grant to York University School of Business Administration to establish a nine-week course for 40 middle managers this summer. Again, that will include attachment to a Canadian firm for practical experience. There is funding for a Canadian expert who will serve as an advisor on privatization to the Government of Poland.
How can anyone sincerely say that there is a lack of initiative? These are very good examples of Canadian foreign policy success, the kind of things that our country is sought out for and appreciated for in the councils of the nations. Canada does not go to other countries with a blueprint of how they should run themselves. We go and work co-operatively with them. They know what their needs are and we have practical experience and technical assistance, as well as financial aid, that can be supportive of what they are doing. We support what they are doing because for years we have sought it, we have urged it, and we have worked for it. In this transformation, we are seeing countries going from totalitarian regimes to democratic regimes, from communist one-party states to pluralistic multi-party states, from the command economy to the market economy, and from harsh militarism and cold war division to a new era of exchange, dialogue, and common security. That is the transition and it is a transition in which Canada is playing an important role as a partner.
We have assisted the central and east European countries in becoming integrated into western markets. We are actively encouraging Canadian trade and investment. Last Saturday, at the Etobicoke-Lakeshore conference on eastern Europe, a number of examples were given of Canadians who are over there doing just these things.
The member for Winnipeg South Centre lamented the difficulty of dealing with bureaucracies. That is a very real problem and no one is underestimating that. It takes a lot of time to place a phone call, let alone to get governmental decisions. But these are things that, in the more traditional areas of trade promotion, we are continuing to pursue very actively. These are positive initiatives.
Supply
The Secretary of State for External Affairs hosted a series of joint venture and investment seminars on Poland. He held them in Montreal, Toronto, and Calgary in January of this year, following through on the arrangements made in November in Moscow when he and the Prime Minister were there. There is no lack of action and no lack of initiative, but a methodical, consistent effort to move on in this era of transition.
The department is getting very practical in this area. It has produced a very useful booklet. I do not know how many members who are criticizing the government for lack of initiative have read it. It is called: A Guide to Business Opportunities in Poland. This is exactly the kind of thing that the former minister did not hear when the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke. He is not hearing it now because, where there is no willingness to hear, there will be nothing heard.
Canadians are actively pursuing opportunities in eastern Europe, whether it be through education, new economic activity, business opportunities, supporting democratic reforms, or working within NATO and other organizations for military climate change. Those people do know. We have passed beyond rhetoric to bringing in an new order here.
We have signed or are signing double taxation and foreign investment protection agreements with countries in eastern and central Europe in order to promote further Canadian investment. The negotiation and signing of those treaties is a response. That is a Canadian initiative.
So, let us not hear any more from those who are timid in their evaluation of Canadian effort. There is nothing wrong with what we are doing, other than our perpetual Canadian capacity to sell ourselves short and to see the glass as being half empty instead of half full.
We have extended the general preferential tariff status to countries like Poland, Hungary, and Romania to help them get better access to the Canadian market. These are initiatives. This is positive action by the government facing the new realities in central and eastern Europe.
The Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State for External Affairs held meetings with 35 Canadian business leaders at the end of April, continuing the process of implementation and carrying through, in order to signal our government's intention to expand the program in this area. That is what we are doing.

May 31, 1990
Routine Proceedings
The member said there is no way that Canadian effort is being co-ordinated. Has he not heard of the formation of the task force on central and east Europe? It is not sitting at External Affairs over in the Lester B. Pearson Building on Sussex Drive, but right here in downtown Ottawa where other departments can be readily involved in its activities and where Canadians from across the country and foreign visitors who are here can deal with it. This is a great effort to bring together, in a concerted way, the initiatives that we are taking.
At the meeting at the end of April, it was agreed that the Canadian government should concentrate on technical assistance and management training, exactly the things I have been mentioning. It was also agreed that we should take a prudent approach at this time and avoid committing large sums of money. Rather, we should facilitate a program that will develop all kinds of connections and linkages between Canadians and the people in those countries, not just government to government, but individual to individual and organization to organization.
The work of the York University Professor Michel Chevalier in developing twinnings between Canadian community colleges and regions in eastern Europe and the U.S.S.R. is very important for the technical training of people. The Fund for Democracy, developed by a number of people of Czechoslovak background who are now Canadians, has gathered from the private sector across the country funds, supplies, and teachers who are in Czechoslovakia teaching the English language.
Last Saturday at the conference in Etobicoke-Lake-shore, one of the organizers of that Fund for Democracy explained that over $7 million in goods and services have already been made available in Czechoslovakia. It is not only the governments but many other organizations that are developing this entire network. That is the strength of relations at many levels between sovereign countries. The network we are weaving together is fundamental and it is certainly a good example of the many initiatives which our government is taking. It is a positive response. For once let us, as Canadians, start to celebrate some of the successes of our foreign policy.
I am not sure how much time I have left, Mr. Speaker, but I have been informed that the parliamentary secretary would like to raise a point of order at this time. I will yield the floor to him.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the previous speaker to comment on any political changes that may have taken place over the past year or several months leading up to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have put such clarity into our proceedings at this juncture that no one could be misguided as to where we are.
In answering the question from the member for Victoria-Haliburton, I would like to say that it is very important that we do look at the political changes as well as the economic changes. It is a fundamental part of Canadian foreign policy that we see political rights and economic changes as being very closely linked.
Just a year ago in China, for example, after a decade of economic change but a failure to have the political change and the individual rights going along with it, there was a real problem because reform and progress cannot march on one leg, it must march on the two together.
In the political changes as well as the economic changes, Canada has been quite actively participating in central and eastern Europe. We are developing a political co-operation program that will ensure that the democratic gains can be sustained in this period of turbulence and radical transformation in a lot of these countries where there have not been free elections for half a century or more.

May 31, 1990
Supply
We are looking at the judiciary, law reform, elections, human rights and the media. Again, these are areas where Canada can provide some specific technical information, assistance and support. Other areas include co-operation on financial planning, health services, environmental concerns-which is desperately needed-and telecommunications, another area of great Canadian strength.
Beyond that there are a lot of really specific detailed initiatives that we have taken to see that Canada is in there and working where it counts, supporting those countries which need the help and responding to their requests. The $40,000 which has gone to Radio-Canada International for equipment and training for the radio networks in Czechoslovakia, Hungary and Poland would be one example. Another would be disposable syringes and further medical supplies to meet the immediate health requirements of Romania. We provided over $500,000 worth of that. Elections Canada provided over $200,000 of financial assistance to Czechoslovakia for the holding of their free elections.
The member for Victoria-Haliburton would also appreciate knowing that we have done little things like providing a $7,000 computer in Bulgaria to help them run their election. We even provided the paper for it. These things may seem pretty trivial when we are talking about some of the global changes, but in fact that is once again where Canadians come through; with the specifics on time, in place and where they are needed. That was the same reasoning that led us to put $10,000 worth of books in the main library at Bucharest University to help replace a lot of the collection that had been destroyed by fire during their revolution in December.
There are programs of training and information exchange on parliamentary procedures. This is something of interest again to all members of Parliament. The Speaker of the House of Commons has been having interns from some of these countries come here to observe the procedures and methods that we follow. The first of these programs was with Poland in March of this year. Our Speaker is currently arranging to have a group from Czechoslovakia following their election on June 8.
These are further examples of the positive initiatives that cause me to say with pride that, yes, Canada is responding in a way that is consistent with the longstanding foreign policy of this country to help other countries help themselves.
Again, we do not have a blueprint of how others should run themselves. We are happy to work with them and provide real support to go beyond nostalgia to a new order.

Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary secretary has just given us, I would say, a puffed up list of things that the government has been doing. He has addressed particularly the situation in eastern European countries and almost totally neglected in his litany what Canada might be doing in the Soviet Union.
He criticizes us on this side of the House for talking about a glass being half empty rather than half full, saying that we were taking a negative perspective of things. I have returned from the Soviet Union and the feeling there that was expressed to us was that the half glass has evaporated.
I wonder, just as a beginning point, what this government is considering doing with our diplomatic presence in the Soviet Union. Obviously to be more of a presence to the Soviet Union and to help them we must have more of a presence within the country and exhibit in that way our commitment to a relationship with the Soviet Union.
It was most unfortunate that when the President of the Soviet Union, President Gorbachev, was here, he did not address this House. I wonder if he felt that he did not know what to address. His comment when our Prime Minister was there was, "What kept you? Why weren't you here before?" The sense there is that there is a lack of communication, there is a lack of commitment. We have made overtures but they have resulted in nothing. I do not know what the parliamentary secretary would have to respond to that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member talks about lack of communication following two days of discussions between our Prime Minister and our Secretary of State for External Affairs with President Gorbachev and Foreign Secretary Shevardnadze here in our capital. I do not know what she wants in the way of communication that would surpass that. That is at the highest level but it reflects that there is, throughout the system, an awful lot of discussion and dialogue taking place that two years ago no one even contemplated.



*

May 31, 1990

The business council between Canada and the U.S.S.R. was specifically created by our government's initiative not to see the Canadian government doing everything there but to put in place a framework where Canadian business people and entrepreneurs could themselves move into that situation. Just as they have found abysmal failure in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe with state directed economies, we have long recognized the importance of the market economy and having our entrepreneurs there. So our government is creating the framework for Canadians to be in there.
The list of specific examples that I was able to give could have gone on but we all speak under time limits here. If she thinks that is a puffed up account, then I am really going to listen with great interest to the substance of her speech which the House will be hearing in a few moments, because I really do lament that someone would look at the specific examples that I have given of Canadian public servants, Canadian business people and educators who are over there. They are travelling as well as the member to the Soviet Union and to places in eastern and central Europe. They are doing a great deal. A lot of them spoke with the eloquence of practical action about the things that they are doing.
To answer the final point of her intervention on diplomatic representation, Canada is very well served by our representatives at our embassy in Moscow. We are looking to expand that with the full service of the consulate in Kiev. The progress in opening that has not been as rapid as any of us would have wanted and we are redoubling our efforts on that.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps nothing better demonstrates to any of us how difficult it really is to move on the ground in some of these countries than the amount of time it has taken to open the consulate. We are committed to doing that. It will happen, there is no doubt about that, but it is not the same as opening a business office in Vancouver. We are dealing with a very different set up and arrangement on the ground. There are a lot of problems that any Canadian would not think would even be a surprise. There are real problems and we are working to overcome them.
I hope that members of the Canadian Parliament would find it in their hearts to be encouraging and
Supply
supportive so that the real progress is recognized. Let us have more ideas about the next steps to take rather than lamenting the good steps that have already been taken.
