Mr. Speaker, I want to pose a question to the parliamentary secretary. Our government has been admonished by not only this Liberal member but by the member for Winnipeg South Centre. I want to deal specifically with agriculture initiatives. The member for Winnipeg South Centre indicated that the Dutch were into one of the countries and had a model program going there.
Will the parliamentary secretary give the House a bit of detail on how many farmers will benefit from the initiative that our government is taking. How many farmers will benefit from that program and about how many Canadian dollars are being spent on those kinds of agricultural initiatives?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question sounded specific enough but the answer, I am afraid, has to be fairly general because we are talking about initiatives in a lot of different countries. For example, a number of Polish farmers will be coming to Canada this year for training, the cost of that being absorbed by the Government of Canada. There is obviously some economic benefit from that. I think that is almost secondary to the training and experience those farmers will get.
If you look at it the other way, what we have been sending to Poland in terms of food aid, while there is a specific figure in the amount of $12 million, the money spent here on such things as pork, canola seed, oil, wheat has gone to the market.
The Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds is currently leading a delegation of industry representatives to Moscow and Geneva to discuss these issues. He will be looking at the terms of grain sales agreements between Canada and the Soviet Union. The member for Winnipeg South Centre dismissed any government action. In fact, here is a trade mission on its way to deal exactly with what the Secretary of State reported progress on this morning.

May 31, 1990
Supply
The existing agreement calls for a minimum purchase of 25 million tonnes of Canadian wheat and feed grains over a five-year period. It can be seen from that alone that there is significant continuing activity.
Not only the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds, but the Minister of Agriculture was in Poland some weeks ago-and with a name like Mazankowski, I think we are all proud to have our agriculture minister go to Poland-when it was announced that Canada would be sending food aid in the amount of $72 million through the stabilization program for Poland.
There are a lot more details and I am glad to have a chance to provide a few of them. The story is a good one. My plea is a simple one. There are successes in Canadian foreign policy in this area and it is high time we all recognized that fact.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to stand today to speak to the motion of our party before the House.
I want to address the events taking place in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. I regret the lack of clear policy by the government in defining a new Canadian role in response to events there.
I want to confine my remarks to defining the new Canadian role in response to events taking place in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union.
I begin my comments this afternoon by stating that, with other members of the external affairs committee, having studied Canada's relation to east Europe and the Soviet Union, I am particularly concerned with Third World affairs, but very interested in the changing role of Canada in the world vis-a-vis east Europe and the Soviet Union. I came away from meetings on my recent trip to the Soviet Union and the Germanys with the sense that the world is wondering what Canada is doing.
Although many Canadians are not that aware of it, the world knows what is going on in Canada. Very often throughout our questioning of newly elected deputies in the Soviet Union and East Germany, many of the questions that we had about unity, disunity, coming together, falling apart, in some instances came back to haunt us. The east Europeans said "Well, what are you doing in Canada?" Canada is the country that is supposed to be exemplar in the world, that brings together so many cultures and religions and has lived harmoniously. They know what is happening here. They look to us for an example. I hope in the coming days we will not prove them wrong.
Besides wondering what is happening within our country, there is a sense of wonderment beyond that. There is a sense that Canada has lost its prestige in the international world, that Canada is becoming marginalized, that Canada is a spectator rather than an actor in what is happening on the world stage, that Canada is not being as creative, visionary and responsive to changing circumstances as it could be. These facts I listen to and watch. I believe that there is quite a bit of truth to them. It is very important for Canada to define a new role in response to events that are occurring around this world, particularly in east Europe, the Soviet Union and with the unification of the Germanys. We are lagging behind and must do more to show our commitment to the change that is occurring and to help to ensure that that change is for the benefit of all of the people of those countries and regions of the world.
I would like to quote from the speech by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that was alluded to by my colleagues earlier. I think it brings to us as Canadians many points with which I can agree. There does seem to be a lack of coherence in government policies addressing many of the points that he raises.
In his speech in Toronto of last Saturday, he said: "Virtually no other nation possesses the web of intense personal connections to eastern and central Europe which we have in Canada. That gives us a special interest and a special capacity in helping those societies become prosperous and free."
After visiting the Soviet Union, you realize just how much we share in common with the Soviet Union with it being a multicultural, multi-ethnic, a country of many diverse religions such as we have in Canada. Through their lack of freedom, however, they have not had the opportunities to express the tolerance that we have in Canada. We are a diverse society. For example, Canada has the largest Ukrainian population outside the Soviet Union.
This week we met with Armenian Canadians. We have some Canadian citizens who understand the culture and the language that is represented by the many republics in the Soviet Union. Canada should take advantage of these characteristics and promote relations in as many diverse ways as possible. This is something that Cana-
May 31, 1990

dians we do not recognize and are not taking full advantage of.
"Canada's stake in Europe should not be taken for granted", our Secretary of State for External Affairs went on to say. This is certainly the truth but what we are doing in actuality would not suggest the veracity of this statement. As said before, there is a feeling in the Soviet Union and the Germanys that Canada is sitting back and waiting to see what is going to happen before taking sufficient action.
The minister went on to say: "Canada's wishes will not necessarily determine Canada's role. Powerful new economic and political forces are at work, forces over which Canada has limited influence." Canada has the potential for much more influence in the situation in east Europe and the Soviet Union than we exhibit by our actions right now. Because of our characteristics and because of our training capacities in many areas, we can contribute.
I come back to some of the specific ways that the Soviet Union and the Germanys asked us to become involved; some of the ways that were expressed to us and some of the ways that seem obvious to us where Canada could improve its role. I go back to my critical remarks about our diplomatic presence in the Soviet Union. I raised this yesterday in the House in a standing order. I recognize that our embassy in Moscow has gone through difficult times with the recall of nine staff people who were well qualified.
With no more cost whatsoever involved, our government ought to make a commitment to putting personnel into our embassies who are fluent in Soviet languages, not just one Soviet language but Soviet languages. If we cannot communicate with people on the street, if we become isolated in our embassies and within the diplomatic community, we are going to be unable to influence change in the Soviet Union as is required.
Without language, without knowledge of Soviet culture and Soviet ways, we simply cannot succeed. When meeting with people in the Soviet Union, they spoke to us of the different ways in which they felt Canada could become involved. As one steps off the plane in the Soviet Union, the very first thing that confronts you is the environment.
Supply
It is interesting that the first words we heard President Gorbachev speak when he arrived in Canada was how clear our air was. He suggested that our Prime Minister ought to tax it. I was very happy to hear that our Prime Minister had no intention of doing that. But I found it very telling that that would be President Gorbachev's first perspective of our country. In reverse, my first impression after arriving in the Soviet Union was the awful environmental problem they have.
The very air one breathes is obviously polluted. In fact, we learned of the very few people we have in our embassy in Moscow, there are two adults who have been there a year and a half and have developed allergies. These people who never had allergies before. This speaks, from their point of view, of the dreadful situation of pollution that exists in that country.
Pollution is in the air and in the water. It is obvious it is there, but the impact of the environmental degradation is not really appreciated or studied. Certainly, the average person in the Soviet Union does not seem to be aware of the environmental degradation.
The main problem in the environment to which they allude with some regularity is the Chernobyl disaster and its massive negative impact on their society. However, even acknowledging the environmental disaster, there is a frustration on behalf of the Soviet people about dealing with the situation. In fact, the tendency appeared to us to be more one of wanting to ignore the problem and get on to other issues which were seen to be more significant.
My impression was that there was a lot that Canada could do to work with the Soviet Union to try to help those people overcome their environmental problems. At the same time, it would help us, as was mentioned by a previous speaker, to be more aware of our own environmental problems. Through co-operation, we could achieve a better environment for the whole world. As we all know, environment knows no borders. When one sees what is happening there and know that the same degradation can be affecting the quality of our life here, it behoves us to urgently address the situation.
We were specifically asked for assistance in agriculture. The thought was that the agricultural system in Canada is excellent. President Gorbachev visited Canada previously in his capacity as Minister of Agriculture and was very impressed with what we were doing. It was felt

May 31, 1990
Supply
that in the areas of food distribution and processing, we would have a lot to offer to the Soviet Union.
Having visited the market in Kiev, where one was beginning to see a slight move to the free market economy in terms of being able to sell excess produce, one realizes what a difficulty they had with food distribution. Some of the sellers in the market had travelled
6,000	kilometres by plane with lemons and oranges from the south to sell at 5, 7 or 10 roubles each. They were able to bring the fruit in suitcases by plane and make a profit. There were serious problems there. We were devastated to hear that the Soviet Union was contemplating nuclear testing in the north. It requested economic assistance and assistance with joint ventures.
The parliamentary secretary has talked about what is being supposedly supported in this country in terms of joint ventures in the private sector, but we know that there are many industries and businesses in the private sector in Canada that have tried unsuccessfully to negotiate business in the Soviet Union but have felt that Canada has not provided sufficient seed money or guarantees to make business possible. There is much more wc can be doing in this way.
Human resource development is seen as a priority and a must particularly in management no matter what the business is, including agriculture, but there is the thought that management development should be linked to joint ventures so that the management training has discipline and focus to it.
We talked to many newly elected deputies who spoke to us of their bewilderment about Canada's role within their country, being aware of the fact that our Prime Minister had visited the country and had signed 14 agreements. They seem to have gone into limbo as far as they were concerned. The half glass of water had evaporated. They were asking us what had happened.
There is a definite lack of communication between this government and the governments of the Soviet Union. There is a lack of communication and a lack of consultation and certainly we in this House have felt that lack of communication and consultation as well in terms of eastern Europe and the Soviet Union.
We hope that our study of the last year will have an impact on what our policies will be in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe, but there should be regular consultation and communication on a regular basis between parliamentarians and the Department of External Affairs.
One of the concerns I have is Canada's difficulty in defining a new role in response to the events there. We have within our own government conflicting views of what we should be doing. Recently we have noticed this conflict in regard to NATO. The Minister of National Defence responded to questions during Question Period of May 17 as follows:
As a mix of deterrents in the defensive alliance, NATO, we have to
maintain the mix that has been successful in keeping peace in Europe
for 45 years.
That was the Minister of National Defence. Yet, we have the Secretary of State for External Affairs saying that NATO must review urgently and comprehensively all aspects of its nuclear and conventional strategy.
It makes little sense to retain nuclear weapons whose only target can be our new friends in Poland, Czechoslovakia, and East Germany. It makes little sense to retain a military strategy which is based on a scenario of a surprise attack across a front which no longer exists and where surprise is no longer possible. It makes little sense to continue to retain in Europe the largest peacetime deployment of military force in the history of the world.
We have conflict among the departments of this government in terms of defining our Canadian role in response to changing events in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. We cannot possibly develop the proper policies when we have these conflicts that the government itself is not resolving. Certainly there is a lack of coherence in policies among departments. My studies in the area of international human rights have certainly highlighted this.
One of the issues that I would like to address briefly before leaving this subject is security and Canada's relationships with eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. We all realize that the military security risk has diminished tremendously with the new peace initiatives glas-nost and hopefully perestroika in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe. However, we hope that with the diminishing of the military security risk east-west, there will be peace dividends deriving from this in a north-south direction.
May 31, 1990

The security issue is now north-south rather than east-west. The world must recognize that as much effort must be put into keeping peace in a north-south direction where it is not so much arms-but that is not out of the question-but poverty which is a security risk, the new greatest threat to our world, and environmental degradation which we are all so concerned about derives from poverty. There are many ways that Canada can define its role with changing events in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. We must not be the lazy fat cat that sits back watching what is going on. Rather, I believe Canada can be the mouse that roared.
An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. We must act now to help move toward peace and security with changes in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe right now by doing everything we can to hasten that process.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment my colleague on an excellent address which covered many of the aspects of our relationship with the Soviet Union and eastern Europe.
It is clear that her recent visit to those countries has been a source of enrichment in terms of her understanding of the problems confronting them and how Canada can effectively contribute to their solution.
I would like to ask her to draw upon her experiences during her recent trip to comment on a few specific aspects, particularly in light of the comments during debate today, about the Canadian presence in the Soviet Union not keeping up with the new demands that have been placed upon it.
Based on her recent trip and her observations made in Moscow and other parts of the Soviet Union, what new demands are being placed on our diplomats and foreign service people in the Soviet Union? Where is the most urgent need for us to beef up our presence and facilitate the transition which is taking place in that country?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question. Other than the environment being one of the first things that struck us on arrival in the Soviet Union, the second was that we had so little staff in our embassy there. We were very grateful for their gracious hosting of our group and for their great effort to make us
Supply
comfortable and to make our meetings and visit profitable. I believe that happened.
However, we also felt that they were working under severe neglect and circumstances that could be corrected. It is very difficult to go into a situation such as exists in the Soviet Union and integrate oneself, make valuable contacts, and be able to negotiate with the people if one cannot speak the language and does not fully understand their culture.
We do know there was a diplomatic furore some months ago which caused some well qualified people in our embassy there to leave the country. I think that our Department of External Affairs should look at the qualifications of staff going to our embassies and consulates.
There is supposedly a consulate opening in Kiev. It has been delayed, but I have a sense from talking to people in the mission there that perhaps the necessary aggressive action was not being taken on the part of our government to push for the opening of that consulate.
It was also obvious that we needed a consulate in Leningrad, one of the chief economic regions of the Soviet Union. We heard earlier from another colleague of the general lack of consulates and embassies in east Europe and the Soviet Union.
There was the sense in West Germany that Canada could be doing a lot more in East Germany through West Germany. In that embassy we need a lot more Canadian facilitators who speak German and who speak languages of east European countries. We have those resources in our country because of our multicultural nature. Mr. Speaker, you know those resources are here. We should be capitalizing on them to augment and improve our way of relating and carrying on business in that part of the world.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Erie.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the applause. It should encourage me to deliver a speech today that will be earth shattering, people moving, and whatever else goes with it.
I am grateful for the opportunity to address the House today on the very topical question of east Europe and our policies in defence, trade, and foreign affairs. I do not think any members of the House have been anything

May 31, 1990
Supply
short of captivated by the startling events which have swept through the Soviet Union and eastern Europe.
I listened fairly closely to the speeches delivered by the hon. member for Northumberland and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. Though I want to develop my speech today around defence issues primarily, I want to touch on a couple of economic issues.
I brought with me two or three news releases. This is something the House is already aware of. It is history, but I want to bring forward that these are initiatives that the government has taken. We have not been asleep at the switch:
Minister Signs Protocol with the Soviet Union Ottawa, Sept. 11, 1989 -
I am reading from the press release:
-Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Agriculture, Don Mazankowski loday officially concluded negotiations under the Fourth Canada-U.S.S.R. Mixed Agricultural Commission-in Moscow-the focus of the 1989 MAC was decidedly commercial - While we are anxious to transfer our technological expertise, our business community must take the lead in determining the conditions of the agreement.
Another one reads:
Deputy Prime Minister to Lead Business Delegation to Poland
Ottawa, March 27, 1990 -Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Agriculture-will lead a delegation of senior Canadian business people on a trade and investment mission to Poland, April 4-7 -
"Our primary goal for this mission is to develop economic and trade co-operation -and to encourage a broader range of contacts-
Then the April 2, 1990 press release reads:
Mayer to Discuss Trade Issues in Moscow and Geneva
-Grains and Oilseeds Minister-Mayer is leading a delegation of industry representatives to Moscow and Geneva to discuss trade issues this week.
Mr. Mayer will be in Moscow until April 4 -
The conclusion of that page reads:
Accompanying Mr. Mayer in the Soviet Union are Bill Reid of Canadian Bronze, Pat Shimbashi of Diamond S Products and Paul Klein of the Winchester Group.
This indicates to all of us that there have been economic initiatives by the government to see that there will be trade with what has been known as the Warsaw Pact countries. Initiatives are being taken. As a result of
this there are and will be tremendous opportunities available to Canadians. I think it is important that we put that on the record today.
I want to read in part the opposition motion today which says that it regrets that there is a lack of clear policy by the government to address the serious issues of trade, commercial relations, and agricultural agreements. What utter nonsense for the opposition to make statements like that when we have the proof positive right here. The proof is in the pudding and we have it. We have been taking initiatives.
One is absolutely right if someone is going to ask: "Have you done all you can do?" Absolutely not. There is much more that can be done. That is a big piece of geography. We are looking at a population in eastern Europe that would give us a tremendous amount of opportunity for us to sell our products and sell our expertise. I know that as Canadians we are going to accept that challenge.
The member for Northumberland had charged us with not being responsible for filling the need for diplomatic officials in Russia and in some of the other countries. I think that is true, but we have not been asleep at the switch. I was pleased that she had the honesty to say that we have to bear in mind that some of these officials had to leave Russia. It is going to take time for us to fill those vacancies and I know we are going to follow through. We also need to put that in the context of the dramatic changes that have taken place in eastern Europe which have happened so quickly.
I would differ with the opposition motion not only in those initiatives that we have taken in agriculture and other commercial initiatives, but with the claim that the government has not been clear in setting out the impact of these momentous changes on Canadian policy.
I would submit that Canada, acting in concert with NATO allies, has been consistent and constructive in adapting our policies to those recent developments. The changes which have transformed eastern Europe and the Soviet Union just over this past 12 months have truly been startlingly.
May 31, 1990

In essence, the process of foreign and domestic policy reform in these countries will redraw the political landscape of Europe as we have known it since 1945, four and a half decades. There are new governments in Poland, East Germany, Hungary and Czechoslovakia. We have witnessed the fury of the Romanian revolution which deposed the Ceausescu regime.
Finally, there is the prospect of German reunification, possibly the most concrete sign that the cold war is fading into the annals of history. Far from being unsettled by these developments, Canada and the other alliance countries are encouraged by the spread of democracy and political independence to the eastern European countries. These recent developments have the potential to bring to fruition NATO's long standing goal of a more genuine and lasting peace on the European continent.
For the NATO countries, an essential part of this more stable peace lies in the speedy conclusion and implementation of an agreement on conventional forces in Europe currently under negotiation in Vienna, the so-called CFE agreement.
The impact of this agreement and its accompanying regime of intrusive verification on European security will indeed be enormous. Once implemented, the prospective CFE agreement will drastically reduce the possibility of surprise attack and large scale offensive action, something which has been a fundamental NATO arms control objective from the very beginning.
Although both sides have made much progress toward an agreement, some important issues remain to be settled and the NATO countries call on the Warsaw Pact nations to work with the alliance in resolving these remaining issues.
Canada also believes that the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe should play a much larger role in facilitating a more just and a more stable peace on the continent. As my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, noted in a speech at the University of Toronto last weekend: "The role of the CSCE must now be expanded so that it becomes a drawing board for the new European architecture. As a complement to NATO, the CSCE can become a true instrument of
Supply
co-operative security, one which would supplement deterrence with reassurance". Similar sentiments on the role of the CSCE were expressed by the NATO defence ministers in their final communique of the recent Defence Planning Committee meeting in Brussels.
It is precisely because the events of the last 12 months have been so fundamental in their impact that we are able to contemplate these happy prospects. At the same time, we must be realistic about some of the dangers which still face us. There remain aspects of the European security environment which call for us to be both prudent and deliberate as we contemplate how we might change the structures of western security, structures which have served us so well over the past four decades.
First of all, it is important to remember that even after the implementation of a CFE agreement, the Soviet Union will retain the most powerful conventional and nuclear forces in Europe. We need to remind ourselves of that fact. This underlines the need for western countries to continue the type of successful collective defence arrangements that NATO has embodied for this past 40 years.
Certainly no one will lament the passing of the cold war, but drawing down the military stand-off in Europe will require a disciplined, co-ordinated effort on the part of the NATO countries so that at each stage of this process, the alliance can retain military forces which are adequate to its security requirements.
In the wake of the CFE agreement, some reduction in defence spending can be expected, and NATO recently decided that its long-standing goal of having alliance defence budgets grow at an annual rate of 3 per cent is no longer appropriate. However, although the precise levels will vary with national circumstances, the determining factor for the alliance countries will continue to be the ability to field forces which are adequate to NATO's missions of deterrence and of defence. We should also remember that there will be substantial costs attached to the verification and to the implementation of the CFE treaty itself.
To return to the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on May 26, I quote: "Twelve months does not invalidate the lessons of history. The possibility of instability is there and Soviet military capabilities

May 31, 1990
Supply
remain substantial. Therefore, a strong military mandate for NATO continues to be valid and the North American commitment to Europe represented by the presence of Canadian and American troops there is crucial as we strive for strategic stability at significantly lower levels of military force".
Beyond the need to maintain a stable military balance in Europe, it is important for us to remain aware that rapid and fundamental change, the sort that we are witnessing today in Europe, can be an inherently unstable process. To ensure that the changing nature of European politics remains on a peaceful path, NATO can and indeed should remain a cornerstone of European security, providing a body where some difficult western security issues, from arms control to German unification, can be dealt with in a co-ordinated fashion.
In summary, the alliance has committed itself to seizing the current opportunities to further its longstanding goal of a more stable peace in Europe, one where military forces are required only to prevent war and to ensure self-defence. NATO will retain its general principles of deterrence and defence, but will do so with the lowest possible force levels and a strategy which is appropriate to the new circumstances.
Thus, when representatives from the alliance countries convened the recent nuclear planning group meeting at Kananaskis, Alberta, they reaffirmed NATO's need to base its security on an appropriate mix of nuclear and conventional forces. I must emphasize that throughout the troubled history of East-West relations, nuclear weapons have provided a very powerful inhibition to military conflict, and in my view, the alliance is correct to retain nuclear weapons as an integral part of its deterrent posture for the foreseeable future.
At the same time, however, the alliance agreed that the recent developments in Eastern Europe, coupled with the improving prospects for conventional arms control, suggested a diminishing need for NATO to field short-range nuclear forces. Consonant with this perception, Canada and the other alliance countries welcomed the Bush administration's decision to terminate the modernization of nuclear artillery shells deployed in Europe as well as the development of the follow-on-to-Lance missile.
The nuclear planning group communique welcomed the accelerated timetable for negotiations to reduce land-based short-range nuclear missile systems deployed in Europe, which should commence after the signing of the CFE agreement. As the Soviet Union enjoys a substantial superiority in these systems, NATO reiterated its call for the Soviet Union to carry out substantial reductions in these systems.
At the recent defence planning committee meeting in Brussels, the NATO defence ministers noted that the radical changes in Eastern Europe made it essential that the alliance review its broader military strategy. This review will assess what NATO's defence posture should be in terms of force levels and operational doctrines.
In their final communique the defence ministers went on to say the following:
The alliance is entering a new decade in which it will face unprecedented change and opportunity. In the midst of change, the need for an established and reliable system of collective security will remain undiminished. We shall therefore hold fast to the basic principle of war prevention through deterrence and defence. In adapting our defence efforts to meet the needs of a changing world, we shall ensure that the levels, structures, and operational concepts of our armed forces continue to evolve in a positive and constructive way.
The alliance has already begun to move in this direction. This year's NATO summit, to be held in early July, will consider NATO's role in the transformed Europe of the 1990s. At a more concrete level, the alliance has taken a number of steps which will lower the peacetime readiness of its forces, including changes in its training programs and significant cuts in the size and number of military exercises. Quite apart from the confidencebuilding effect these measures will have, they will also reduce the impact of NATO's military forces on the public, benefit the quality of life, and protect the environment. I think hon. members will agree that these are important components of the much discussed peace dividend.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, this demonstrates that the alliance is adapting with both prudence and with vision to the sweeping changes in Eastern Europe and the uncertain future of European security. In responding to these new developments, NATO does not simply seek to jettison the past for the sake of public relations. Instead, the alliance seeks to adapt its existing policies, those which have provided for the successful management of western security for the past 40 years, in ways which will
May 31, 1990

allow it to contribute to the forging of a more stable and a more lasting peace. Canada, we are proud to say, has been an integral part of this process and fully supports these recent NATO initiatives.
In conclusion, I want to emphasize that, contrary to the erroneous suggestions of some observers, there is no disagreement between the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs on these issues. Canada will continue to play an active role in the alliance as it adjusts to a changing Europe, and every attempt will be made to harmonize Canada's contribution to NATO with the events in Europe and the defence policy review currently under way.

Mr. Speaker, it was hard to believe in some instances that we were together on a trip to the Soviet Union and the united Germanys because the way we approach the issue is so different.
My esteemed colleague referred so often to Canada's role in the alliance as if there was to be no change there. Yet what we heard about was the newglasnost, the desire for perestroika, the desire for changes did not include the emphasis on military security and new alliances.
I would like to ask my colleague if he does not agree that our emphasis should be on trade, commercial relations, Arctic security, agricultural agreements, and the many issues that we talked about when we were overseas. We talked about the need for parliamentary exchanges and that even parliamentarians could learn from each other. In particular, new deputies in the Soviet Union were making this request.
It seemed to me that security in the world today derives from civil, political, social, and economic rights and does not come from the end of a gun. Could my esteemed colleague respond to my reflections?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to respond to the hon. member for Northumberland. Perhaps our differences are not so pronounced after all, for I agree with much of what she has said. We need to consider civil rights and we need to have parliamentary exchanges. That is a tremendous way to acquire an
Supply
education, to learn to meet people's needs, and to understand each other. That is so very important.
Glasnost is occurring. We are now able to see into countries of which we had only a wee glimpse before. Now the doors and windows are opening. I agree with her on all those comments.
Perhaps where we may have some disagreement is that I believe we, as a government and in NATO, know that the U.S.S.R. is still the world's strongest military nation and has this means at its disposal.
History has proven over the last four and a half decades that we have had the preservation of peace in Europe because NATO has been there and we have been strong. We want that peace to continue. Yet, we know that the amount of military forces there will start to diminish. Those numbers will decrease and we welcome that. However, for us immediately to dissolve NATO- and I am not sure that is what the hon. member is suggesting-would not be an honourable or wise course for us to take.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very short question for the hon. member who just spoke and who obviously spoke on behalf of the government. He and I went to the Soviet Union and Germany, and I think he saw for himself how limited the resources of the Department of External Affairs really were. I would like to ask him why, considering increased demand in Soviet Union, our staff, which is barely twenty strong, has not been increased. There was some talk of reassigning certain postings in Western Europe to Eastern Europe. I don't think that is enough, and it's not the right way to proceed. We need additional staff. If Europe 92 is important to the Conservative government, the people who are already there should be left in place, and transfers to Eastern Europe should involve people from headquarters at External Affairs here in Ottawa, if we are to respond to these new demands and obligations.
The hon. member and I also went to Berlin, and we all know that the new dynamics at work in Germany will require particular attention. A number of Western countries have already increased their diplomatic commercial contingent in Berlin.

May 31, 1990
Supply
Unfortunately, Canada has done nothing so far. The number of Canadian representatives posted in Berlin to deal with our needs is still the same as it was several months ago. We are still treating Berlin as an exclusively military mission. I fail to understand this government's failure to respond energetically to new obligations and new trade opportunities for Canada in Eastern Europe and especially in Germany, via Berlin. Could the hon. member give us some good news in this respect or will he at least make a commitment to join me in urging the minister to increase our diplomatic staff in eastern Europe as soon as possible?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel. He has raised some very important and vital issues that our government and Parliament need to address.
Regarding limited staffing, he is absolutely right but, as I indicated to someone else, we need to put that in context. When we look at the events which have unfolded in eastern Europe so quickly in the past 12 months, surely we are not going to be able to respond that quickly to all those changes. The hon. member is aware that some of the diplomatic corps and staff had to leave the U.S.S.R., but that should also be put that on the record as well.
There is no doubt that 1992 is an important year. The possibilities for trade in Europe will be unlike anything we have ever seen before. We as a government need to do everything we can assist people involved in business and people who want to travel. We need do everything we can to see that we get our share of that huge market.
The hon. member mentioned East Germany. It is absolutely going to be a dynamic market for the investment of other countries. We know that. East Germany is going to flourish very quickly because of the reunification and what will take place on July 2 regarding their fiscal agreements.
The returns will be much faster in East Germany. We need to make Canadian business people aware of the tremendous opportunities. In fact, the Germans told us to come into Germany and invest and the returns will be fast.
It is not so in the rest of eastern Europe. The returns there will be much slower. They will be perhaps 10, 15, or 20 years for the returns on investments.
Having been there, I certainly accept the challenge of the hon. member for Papineau-Saint-Michel to make my wishes known to the responsible ministers that we have more people in Europe. We need them. In that regard, I agree with him.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to use this opportunity to speak on foreign policy-a too infrequent opportunity in the House to focus on this topic of major concern to our country and to the world-to make a plea for a more coherent foreign policy, and also a plea that Canada take a more activist, internationalist role.
At least the last portion of this debate has focused on our relations with eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. Of course, that is where all the action has been in the last year. There have been unbelievable developments in that area. But what we have to remember-and this is why I want to talk about the coherence of foreign policy-is that we have gone way beyond our ability to compartmentalize the world. When events happen as they have done in the Soviet Union and in eastern Europe the implications are global. Canada has an absolutely pivotal role in affecting those events and the implications that flow from them.
Canada has a reputation second to none on the international front. Canada has disproportionate influence because of that reputation. There are some, and I consider myself among them, who think that reputation is more as a result of history than as a result of action, at least in the last decade.
As someone who has been active in international development and interested in international affairs for a long time, I feel a good deal of frustration that Canada does not use the influence she has.
I remind the House that Canada is a member of the Commonwealth; the Francophonie; the G-7, the most powerful countries in the world, and has a seat on the UN Security tCouncil. We are the only country in the world that has those kinds of links. We are unique. We are a very humble country, in spite of all this, and I think too humble. We use our influence to too little effect.
May 31, 1990

On this Liberal opposition day, I hope that my contribution to this debate will be to urge Canada to be more activist and more coherent in the development of foreign policy.
Canada should be using its role as a bridge between the developed world and the developing world. As someone who has had the opportunity to travel more in the developing world than in the developed world, I can tell you that Canada has a glowing reputation. I agree with what the Prime Minister said today in his address to the Elouse on the crisis that is confronting us, that the rest of the world looks in amazement that we cannot sort out our own problems.
If we could just step outside ourselves and look at Canada through the eyes of someone from Sudan, Brazil, or El Salvador, the pride that we would feel in what we have achieved would be a motivation to solve our current impasse. But I digress.
Canada should be using its role much more effectively as that bridge between the developed world and the developing world. This is really a global village. When one talks about security and environmental issues, we are in this together and Canada, with its reputation, should be using all those seats, in the Commonwealth, the Francophonie, and the G-7, to a much greater effect.
Our Minister of Finance sits on one of the major councils, the International Monetary Fund. As someone who is on the subcommittee on international debt, I know the kind of influence the International Monetary Fund has in international development and in foreign policy. Foreign policy cannot be distinguished from economic policy or from trade policy. They are all together. That is why I plead for coherence.
We need a vision of what Canada is and of what the world can achieve. This is what I see lacking in Canada now, a lack of vision and direction in foreign policy. It is a tragic loss of opportunity, not just for Canada, but for the world. Canada should be using that role to become not just a peacekeeper. We have a very good reputation in that role. There are many people from my constituency who have served with the armed forces with great distinction in a peacekeeping role; Cyprus is one example. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to address this House, although briefly, on such an important question as Canada's foreign policy, especially as it
concerns the countries of Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union.
Since I have long had a keen interest in this subject, I am sorry that I cannot go into it as deeply as it deserves. Since I was elected to this House, Mr. Speaker, I tell you that in the world today and especially in Canada, our relations with other countries and especially with such an important one as the Soviet Union, as shown by Mr. Gorbachev's visit among us yesterday and the day before, will interest me even more, among my other concerns. I am grateful for the privilege to be able to talk about it briefly today, at least for starters.

I will make a few brief, general remarks which will be more impressionistic than factual in their content about the subject before us today.
The first remark has to do with leadership. I would like to contrast the style of leadership which has emerged in the events that have been taking place in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union with the style of leadership which has been manifested in the reaction to those events in the west. I believe they are telling for us as Canadians and for those living in the western industrialized world as to the kind of way in which we are going to have to react diplomatically to circumstances and to events which will be taking place in the years ahead.
It has been said that the revolution taking place in the Soviet Union has been a revolution from the top down. Clearly there is no doubt that what has captured the imagination of the world has been the style of leadership manifested by Mr. Gorbachev and others who have emerged in the Soviet Union during these last several months to transform the economy, the society, and, indeed, the entire world by the events which have taken place there.
What has characterized the leadership as we have seen of Mr. Gorbachev, which is so much in contrast to traditional diplomacy, has been his willingness to forgo the established patterns of the past, to take amazing political risks, to move forward on all fronts, and to be prepared to risk all, knowing that the transformation of his society really had to take place all at once. We have seen that Mr. Gorbachev has been working feverishly. He has captured our imagination by his ability to do
May 31, 1990

something which no one else has been willing to do. He has been carried forward by events.
I think that is one characteristic which has been manifested in the nature of situation taking place in the Soviet Union. The force of his personal leadership, as well as those of others who have come forward throughout the Soviet Union from all walks of life, has propelled the events that we have seen.
Another aspect of the leadership in the Soviet Union and in eastern Europe is that it has come from unpredictable places. We all know that the origins of many of these events can be traced to the early 1980s in Poland. Who is the person who has been most identified with those events? A shipyard worker, Lech Walesa, who came from nowhere to guide and move the events in Poland through the difficult decade that emerged last year in the democratic reforms which have taken place in that country.
We have seen in the western press observing events in that country just how that particular personality has been transformed by the momentous changes in which he has been involved producing.
If we turn to Czechoslovakia we see that a playwright is now president of that country, someone who has been in exile and in prison for many years under the previous regime. The examples could be multiplied.
What this has shown is the fluid and totally new styles of leadership which the kinds of events taking place in Europe have demonstrated. What has been unfortunate is the cautious, timid reaction in the west. It is more serious than simply wanting to watch and see how the drama in eastern Europe is going to play itself out. It has been marked by an inability to comprehend the complexity of the events taking place in eastern Europe. Perhaps more than typical has been the reaction of Canada which has been so slow in responding to the events that have taken place.
The Prime Minister's visit last November is illustrative of that, if not merely for the fact that it took him so long to get there, a fact which was remarked upon by Mr. Gorbachev himself. He and this government have been so slow to respond to the initiatives which have taken place as a result of that visit.

Canada has much to offer the Soviet Union and eastern Europe in this time of rapid change. We have many interests in common. Whether those initiatives be in terms of collective security, Arctic co-operation, new environmental concerns, or the new environmental imperatives which we now realize are the major issues confronting the planet in the future, we must be prepared to rethink our approaches in a dramatic way. He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to start the debate on second reading of Bill C-201, an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code (scabs and essential services). The purpose of this bill is basically to prohibit Crown corporations from using the services of a person hired for the sole purpose of performing the duties of an employee who is on strike or locked out.
The bill was first tabled in 1987, but unfortunately was not among the winning numbers in the parliamentary lottery during our government's first term. That is why I had to table the bill again in April, 1989.
When the bill was first tabled, it was intended as a way to avoid a recurrence of strikes as problematic and painful for this government as the strikes by letter carriers and postal workers in the spring and summer of 1986. You will recall that at the time, the Canada Post Corporation resorted to hiring scabs right across Canada, mostly young unemployed Canadians, to replace its employees who were legally on strike. This had the effect of worsening the dispute and led to increasingly tragic scenes of violence.
We saw innocent youths enduring insults for the sake of working under terrible conditions for a higher salary than regular employees. It was certainly not an edifying sight to see the lowest paid workers in our society
fighting each other for the sake of a temporary job. These scenes, reminiscent of the 30s and the Depression, are completely out of place in the 90s.
Although it has now been nearly three years since these unhappy events took place, I think that now, more than ever before, the federal government desperately needs an instrument that encourages negotiation instead of confrontation. At a time when the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms is being held high as an example, we have a duty as a government to put an end to situations that are an affront to human dignity and human rights.
The endless dispute at Voyageur, a federally-regulated transportation company but not subject to the Quebec Labour Code or Quebec anti-scab legislation, recently provided us with one more reason to acquire as soon as possible a flexible yet effective instrument for limiting disputes. This particular dispute was settled not long ago, but it went on for more than two years.
This Canadian antiscab legislation stems basically from Clause 97(a) of Bill 45 to amend the Labour Code which was introduced by Pierre-Marc Johnson, the then-Que-bec Minister of Labour, on July 29, 1977.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to summarize some of the arguments in favour of these antiscab provisions about which so much was written about 13 years ago.
These provisions were meant to eliminate one of the major bones of construction in some labour disputes and one of the most apparent sources of frustration and violence during work stoppages. The history of Canadian Labour disputes shows that the systematic imbalance of the parties quickly results in frustration for one of the parties, even both, and ends up in verbal or physical abuse.iolence.
Since the Labour Code granted the right to strike, was it not normal to expect this right to imply the protection of the jobs with which it is associated?
Of course, a small minority of employers use scabs. But to tolerate the backward behaviour of this minority would mean in fact a denial of the basic right to strike.
The data obtained between 1972 and 1980 by the Centre de recherche et de statistiques sur le marche du travail and which can be found in the report entitled Les briseurs de greve et le Code du travail which this Quebec organization published in March 1982, clearly demon-
May 31, 1990

strate that the implementation of the Quebec antiscab legislation had a deterrent effect on employers.
Between 1972 and 1977, fewer than 3 per cent of the disputes in Quebec had seen the hiring of scabs. Bill 45 caused this proportion to fall by half to less than 2 per cent. The data concerning these disputes indicate that among these remaining 2 per cent, employers were mostly ignorant of the legislation and rarely acting in bad faith.
Among federal institutions, it is mostly Canada Post which used scabs over the past ten years. In addition to lowering for long periods of time the level of postal services which the Canadian people had every right to expect, these strikes were a major traumatic experience for Canadians. For a great many senior citizens and people living alone, their mail carrier provides more than a simple service, he is a friend, a witness of better or worste times, a smile which brightens their daily routine. Several of them felt that, when a scab was delivering their mail it was a betrayal of their mail carrier! And yet, waiting for their cheques for some of them might often have been the only adventure in their lives!
Upon reflection, I feel that it would be advisable to extend the application of this future federal antiscab legislation not only to Crown corporations, but to all federally incorporated businesses. This might prevent the deterioration of disputes, as in the case involving the Voyageur Transport Company in Montreal or the Hudson Bay's a few years ago.
It is well known that the Quebec law not only limited the number of conflicts involving strike-breakers but also appreciably reduced the average length of strikes involving scabs. The above-mentioned report points out that since Bill 45 took effect in Quebec, the average duration of these conflicts has fallen from 171 to 111 days, a decrease of 35 per cent, which is quite considerable.
This law has also reduced the number of man-days lost as a result of work stoppages and thus the impact on workers' jobs.
The shorter a conflict, the less likely it is to be violent and lead to a strained atmosphere unsuitable for solving
