conflicts. When the employees go back to work, the climate will therefore be more serene and thus help operations resume more quickly.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that Bill C-201 is in no way meant to prevent the provision of essential services or to prevent companies from continuing operations, but rather to make these essential services more humane.
This bill will not prevent employers from trying to run their business with management personnel or non-striking employees or from calling police or security agencies to protect their property and facilitate access for managers and other employees to the premises.
However, any employer who violates a federal antiscab law would be liable to a fine of $20,000 to $100,000 per day, while employer representatives who agree to use strike-breakers could be fined from $10,000 to $50,000.
Some might fear that under such a law, some companies would have only two choices: to close down or to accept the union's demands. The Quebec experience shows that this argument is invalid, since those companies that closed following legal strikes did so not because they did not call upon strike-breakers but for many other reasons.
I think that our government, just like the Quebec government in 1977, should give labour relations in federal institutions a new orientation. Despite the fears of some, the purpose is not to favour one party over the other, but rather to eliminate as best we can, with the means at our disposal, those things most likely to cause conflict and tension in labour-management relations.
Mr. Speaker, these provisions are meant to protect those who are out on the street to legitimately exercise their right to strike. They protect the dignity of our workers, but their main purpose is to try and put an end to the sorry spectacle of companies who would hire other workers to replace those who are exercising their legal rights.
By restoring a certain balance between the parties and by obliging them to pursue their negotiations in a calmer atmosphere, the government is playing a leading role in changing attitudes.

May 31, 1990
Private Members' Business
Too many employers have been negligent about maintaining this balance during negotiations, an attitude that has not worked out to their advantage.
After all, for an employer the purpose of collective bargaining is to know in advance under what rules and criteria his company will operate during the next two or three years. A collective agreement means that for two or three years, the employer has the assurance he will be able to operate without any problems extraneous to the production process that will prevent his company from functioning properly. Employers who failed to accept these elementary rules of the game have found to their sorrow this has been counter-productive.
At a time of increasing references to new agreements between management and employees, to co-operative management and participation by all workers in company operations-at a time when the emphasis is on the need for providing mechanisms for permanent negotiations; at a time when we try to get everyone more and more involved as employees and as citizens aware of the national issues, I think it is urgent to stop this medieval, outdated procedure of resorting to use of scabs.
In the recent debate on national issues like free trade, the deficit or the new goods and services tax, this government has tried to involve all citizens in a public consultation process so that all Canadians will participate in Canada's economic renewal.
It is with this attitude in mind that we should consider the need for federal anti-scab legislation. If we want Canadian workers to have confidence in their government, we must be able to preserve the most precious attribute they have; their dignity. The right to strike was acquired over the years thanks to the courage of many workers and to their faith in human dignity. It was acquired after bitter struggles, won at great personal cost. It is this fundamental right that is challenged by the use of scabs. By allowing this to happen, the government is indirectly undermining the workers' right to strike. The hiring of scabs in some disputes might jeopardize the right to strike, because a party refuses to accept the rules of the game and tilts in its favour the normal balance of power.
I do not think that the government wishes to rewrite history. Quite the contrary, our government wants to
move forward, toward creativity, technology, and well-designed and more modern management methods.
Far from ruining the good relations between the parties, this bill is meant to re-establish order and strike again a new balance between them.
The parties are responsible for this balance and the success or failure of the bargaining process will hinge on the way they use it.
As I was saying earlier, most strikes and lock-outs end up in service agreements, without the employers using scabs. In a sense, this antiscab bill is more provocative than coercitive.
The purpose of this bill is also to prevent situations from deteriorating and striking workers from breaking material and causing injuries out of frustration.
As I said, the idea is not to go to war against employers, but to impose humane and reasonable conditions during disputes, to create tools to make it possible for striking workers to calm negotiate during strikes and lock-outs without fear of losing their jobs to scabs.
What is important is for the duration of disputes to be restricted so as not to unduly penalize the public, the workers and the corporation. Statistics show that all disputes in which scabs were used lasted a very long time, much too long, Mr. Speaker.
I hope that the House will be interested in this bill and that most members will support it on second reading.

Mr. W.C. Scott (Victoria -Haliburton) Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak today on Bill C-201, introduced for the consideration of the House by the hon. member for Richelieu. The bill is a detailed account that reflects the concerns of the hon. member in dealing with an important subject with both economic and social ramifications.
The bill before the House proposes a number of changes to the Canada Labour Code, Part I, Industrial Relations. Its over-all objective is two-fold. First, it seeks to prohibit the hiring of persons to replace the employees of a Crown corporation who are on strike or are locked out. Second, the bill proposes changes intended to ensure that essential services are maintained
May 31, 1990

in the event of a strike or lock-out in Crown corporations.
I share the sentiments of many members of the House who hold the view that good industrial relations is an essential element of our economic and social fabric and that it can make a meaningful contribution to our economic performance. The preamble to the Canada Labour Code, Part I, Industrial Relations, makes reference to the significance of good industrial relations practices to the economy. It indicates a commitment by Parliament:
- to support labour and management in their co-operative efforts to develop good relations and constructive collective bargaining practices, and deems the development of good industrial relations to be in the best interests of Canada in ensuring a just share of the fruits of progress to all.
The preamble to the code makes clear that there is not only an economic significance to industrial relations but, also, that there is a larger impact that extends to the common good of Canadian society. This is declared in the first paragraph of the preamble which affirms that:
There is a long tradition in Canada of labour legislation and policy designed for the promotion of the common well-being through the encouragement of free collective bargaining and the constructive settlement of disputes.
One of the important elements of the bill before us is the fact that it proposes to make changes to some important industrial relations practices in several industries under the Canada Labour Code, but only to Crown corporations. We must appreciate that the spectrum of industries under the jurisdiction of the code is very broad in scope and covers a wide range of economic and industrial activity.
The range of industries covered by the code's jurisdiction encompasses the different modes of interprovincial and international transportation, including railways, airlines, trucks, and bus transport. Encompassed, as well, are the telephone, telegraph, and cable systems; shipping; longshoring; broadcasting; banking; pipelines; ferries; tunnels and bridges; primary fishing; and most Crown corporations. Also included are certain undertakings that have been declared by Parliament to be for the general advantage of Canada, including grain elevators, uranium mining and processing, and flour and feed mills.
Private Members' Business
This is not to suggest that we should want to see the measures before us applied to all federal jurisdiction industries. On the contrary, measures proposed in the bill present a number of practical difficulties that require the scrutiny of members of the House. But I have to question, in light of the wide range of industries under the code, why Crown corporations should be singled out for special treatment.
I feel certain that significant inequities would arise in the application of our labour relations laws as they apply to industries under the Canada Labour Code if the bill now before us were to be adopted. For example, labour relations at Canadian National Railways and VIA Rail fall under the jurisdiction of the Canada Labour Code and would be encompassed under Bill C-201.
Canadian Pacific Railways is also under the code, but it is not a Crown corporation and would not be covered by the bill. As a consequence, the provisions of the bill would have us accept the view that railway operations under Canadian National are essential while those under Canadian Pacific are not essential.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is another example. It is also a Crown corporation, as we know, with labour relations under the jurisdiction of the Canada Labour Code. Collective bargaining at the CBC would be affected by the proposals included in the bill. Limits would be placed on collective bargaining at the CBC that would not be felt in negotiations at the CTV Network, the Global Television Network, Telemetropole Inc. and other radio and television broadcasting companies under the jurisdiction of the Code that are not Crown corporations.
Miners working for the Cape Breton Development Corporation are under the Canada Labour Code and would be affected by Bill C-201, but workers in similar jobs in the mining industry working for Denison Mines or Rio Algom Mines would bargain under different collective bargaining laws if the bill were adopted. Workers in one company would be treated differently from workers doing similar work in another company in the same industry.
I would submit for the consideration of hon. members that the bill contains an element of arbitrariness in its coverage and that this would create an inequity in the application of the laws governing collective bargaining

May 31, 1990
Private Members' Business
among workers and employees in the federal jurisdiction under the Canada Labour Code.
Another factor I believe should be considered in this regard is the fact that collective bargaining can take place on an industry-wide basis involving one union representing employees working in two or more companies. The most important example that comes to mind would be Canadian National Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway.
These two companies have frequently bargained on a joint basis in past negotiations with nine unions represented by the Associated Railway Unions. Although the approach to bargaining in the railway industry can vary from one round of bargaining to the next, the decision by CN and CP and the union to bargain jointly in this case was in all likelihood taken by the parties in the interest of reaching a collective agreement in the most expeditious manner possible.
The provisions of Bill of C-201, however, would change the framework within which collective agreements negotiations take place and, in doing so, could adversely affect the conditions for determining the most expeditious approach to collective agreement negotiations.
I suggest that we should not want to interfere with the options and the flexibility of the collective bargaining process now available to the parties through the provisions of the Canada Labour Code.
I would like to conclude my remarks by saying that I appreciate the efforts taken by the hon. member in preparing and introducing this bill, and acknowledge the serious attention that he has given to the matter. However, there remains some practical difficulties which will require careful consideration.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA LABOUR CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was asked a short while ago by my colleagues on this side of the House to respond to Bill C-201 and to tell the mover and drafter of this bill our thoughts with respect to its implementation.
First, let me say that as we go through labour codes and legislation as they surround the rights of labour and employers in the country on the federal scale, we find very quickly that there is a great deal of legislation already in place. One wonders if perhaps the legislation
that we are considering today is not duplicated in some other act, for example, the Canada Labour Code, in Sections 2, 4 or 5; the Public Service legislation; or other acts that respect and honour the rights of labour and corporations in the so-called conflicts that always seems to exist between employers and employee in the workforce. I want to compliment the member for having the foresight to bring it forward in this House. He stated that he commenced the movement of this bill in 1986 and for many reasons it did not get to the House. Just recently, in April of this year, he again won the lottery and has the opportunity now to speak to it.
The operative section is Clause 1.1 will come back to that in just a moment. The other operative sections support Section 89 (1.1) right through to Section 90.6. Those and Clause 3 on page 4 of the bill are really the operative sections. Section 100 on to the end of the proposed changes that he is suggesting to the Canada Labour Code are the remedial or penalty sections in this bill. I will come back to section 89 in just a moment.
What is the purpose of the legislation? Obviously this is a bill which is, as it states, to prohibit the hiring of other employees during a strike to replace those employees who are on strike and, second, to ensure that essential services in this country are maintained during the course of a labour dispute. That is the purpose of the legislation and I will refer to that in just a moment or two. However, we do not talk about what is defined as an essential service.
What is this member really trying to do? What mischief is he trying to correct through the introduction of another section of the Labour Code? What is he attempting to make easier within the labour movement and within the structure of our labour-management agreements in this country?
Simply put, this piece of legislation, with which we on this side of the House do not disagree, refers to the problems that were caused in two incidents in the last year or year and a half. One was the post office strike of approximately a year ago. The post office mail carriers had decided to go on strike and the post office started to consider hiring outside people in order to fill the jobs of the letter carriers who were on strike.
The other piece of mischief which I think this bill is trying to correct is what we dealt with in this House in
May 31, 1990

December of this year when the Coast Guard went on strike, prohibited the shipment of grain and caused the closure of the St. Lawrence Seaway approximately 12 or 14 days before the end of the shipping season which prevented all of the grain from the port of Thunder Bay from moving down into the seaway and into the terminals at the downriver ports. As a result, it had to be shipped through the winter by rail at the expense of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. Those are the two incidents of mischief which I think prompted this legislation and which this legislation is designed to correct.
With respect to the Coast Guard strike, Bill C-49, which was passed a short while ago, has corrected that situation. As you will recall, that is back-to-work legislation that was put through this House some 10 or 12 days after the Coast Guard had gone on strike and which returned it to work.
Labour law in this country deals with applications for certification, the certification process itself, the designing and the making up of the bargaining unit and the right to a collective agreement. All of those processes are designed to be embodied in a dispute resolution mechanism that is designed to protect the rights of both the employer and the employee. The basis of that is that every right held by an employer is granted either through the act or through the negotiating process to the employees or the bargaining unit of the employees through the contractual process and then embodied in the collective agreement.
If we do not have the collective agreement in place, we know we do have in our legislation the right of the first contract. Once we have that in place we have another whole dispute resolution mechanism through the grievance procedure, the arbitration and the final award.
With all this legislation, we still have problems. The language of every act has to be so precise, because when it gets to the arbitration process, the whole course of an arbitration can be turned on the wording or interpretation of one section of the act.
If we have any question about this legislation before the House today, it is the imprecision of some of the wording in Bill C-201. I would like to refer to some of these imprecisions. We do not oppose the concept and philosophy of what our colleague is trying to pursue, but we do oppose some of the wording in this bill. We suggest that it should go back to a legislative committee for more in depth study and research.
Private Members' Business
Let me just draw to your attention one of the items that is missing out of the labour code, but which is embodied in the Public Service Staff Relations Act, and that is what we term as a designated employee. When we talk about a designated employee we mean that employee who is responsible for providing essential services within the Canada Labour Code. Section 78 of the code says: "Pursuant to this section the employees or classes of employees in the bargaining unit in this act referred to as designated employees whose duties consist in whole or in part of duties, the performance of which at any particular time, or after any specified period of time, is or will be necessary in the interest of the safety or security of the public."
In my opinion, that is something which should be embodied in the legislation so that we know what we are talking about through this proposed change, that is, what is an essential service. Section 89(1.1), the first part of this proposed legislation, tries to determine what an essential service is but falls a little short of that. Again, that is why I am suggesting that this act should go to a legislative committee for further study.
Another problem that I am having with the interpretation of this act is that it only refers to Crown corporations. As you stated when you were not occupying the chair, Mr. Speaker, and as I have said in my remarks, I suspect that if we pass this legislation or embody the change in the Canada Labour Code, there will be many other corporations put to a disadvantage.
I know my time is running short. Let me just make the point that the other agencies that would be put at a disadvantage would be the other departments of the government that are not Crown corporations, the other agencies that work within the government that are not Crown corporations and the other corporations which are affected by the Canada Labour Code. These include CTV, CPR Rail and so on. Those agencies would be put at a definite disadvantage if this act passes. Therefore, it should go back to the legislative committee for further study.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA LABOUR CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer some observations on the bill before us involving the maintenance of essential services and the prohibition of the hiring of replacement workers where Crown corporation employees are on strike or locked out.

May 31, 1990
Private Members' Business
The present bill provides that where the Governor in Council is of the opinion that a strike in a Crown corporation might endanger the public health or public safety, the Governor in Council may, by order, on the recommendations of the minister, require the maintenance of essential services in the case of a strike.
The concept of danger to public health or public safety can readily be seen to apply to such activities as health, fire and police services.
The Crown corporations that are covered by the Canada Labour Code, Part I, are primarily commercial enterprises, in contrast to the situation provincially. With most federal sector disputes, including those involving Crown corporations, the public consideration is mainly economic in nature.
The impact of work stoppages in such federal Crown corporations as Atomic Energy of Canada, Canadian National Railways, VIA Rail, Cape Breton Development Corporation or the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority would, of course, be evident in terms of the country's or a region's short and long-term economic interest.
The Canada Labour Code sets out a framework which provides mechanisms to minimize work disruptions in industries of national importance, both private and public. Federal undertakings under the code include interprovincial, international rail, road and pipeline transportation; shipping and longshoring; air transportation; telephone, telegraph and cable services; banking; broadcasting; most federal Crown corporations and certain industries declared to be to the general advantage of Canada.
As members of this House know, there have been times when it has been necessary to introduce special back-to-work legislation to end disputes in key areas of economic interest. Such action was taken as a last resort when it became clear that legislative efforts were necessary to provide for the continuation of services essential to the economy.
I will return to the issue of essentiality in a moment, but I would like to explore the implications of the bill proposed to amend the Canada Labour Code which would ban the hiring of replacement workers during strikes or lockouts.
The Canada Labour Code does not prohibit the use of replacement workers in the event of a work stoppage. However, the code does provide certain protective measures for employees affected by labour disputes. Workers engaged in legal strike action cannot be permanently replaced and have the right to return to their employment after a strike in preference to anyone hired to replace them. As well, the code prohibits an employer from disciplining an employee who refuses to perform the task of another who is engaged in a legal work stoppage.
Under the provisions of the Canada Labour Code, the parties are provided conciliation and mediation assistance as required and where appropriate in the interests of dispute resolution. They are encouraged to bargain in good faith and to assess their bargaining priorities in the light of their relative economic strengths and interests.
One of the features of collective bargaining under the code, for both private employers and Crown corporations, is the knowledge of employees and union negotiators, that in the event of a strike, the employer may continue to operate. Such knowledge has a restraining effect on the use of the strike weapon. In the same fashion, the employer seeks to avoid having to deal with disruptive effects of a strike.
It is fundamental to collective bargaining that the parties are encouraged to negotiate and compromise when the facts warrant. In this fashion, tests of economic strength are only used as a last resort. When the union is aware that the employer is not going to be able to maintain operations during a strike, the element of compromise is weakened. On the other hand, if the employer is insured of a minimum workforce, his need to compromise and make concessions is reduced. In effect, the relative power equation is distorted and the carefully balanced approach established under the code is undermined.
In the final analysis, what is at the root of this bill is the question of what in fact is an essential service in the context of the bill and what should the Parliament of Canada do when faced with an important disruption in its area of jurisdiction?
Parliament has adopted the Canada Labour Code which provides for free collective bargaining in federal jurisdiction industries. With this legislation comes the right to engage in legal work stoppages, be it strike or lockout activity. As already noted, the provisions of the Canada Labour Code, which regulate labour-manage-
May 31, 1990

ment relations in the federal sector, place great emphasis on the negotiated resolution of labour disputes. The right to strike or lockout is only acquired after meeting all the dispute resolution requirements of the code.
On those occasions where disputes having major economic importance for Canada cannot be resolved through the normal dispute resolution procedures, the government assesses the facts and circumstances and decides on an appropriate course of action. In the process of analysis, the competing interests of the parties and the public are weighed in the light of the over-all interest. This approach, I believe, is most appropriate for the scope of enterprises covered by the Canada Labour Code.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA LABOUR CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this bill. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Richelieu on it. It is a very precise bill. It deals with a number of issues about the effectiveness of the Canada Labour Code which have been of concern and in need of action for a long period of time.
I cannot agree with the previous speaker that the labour code has established a balance which is acceptable to both the employer and employee in all circumstances. It has a built-in structure which has allowed the less public of the corporations to take advantage of even the definition of essential services.
We are dealing with this bill now at second reading, which is to give it approval in principle. I must again congratulate the member for putting his finger on those items in this bill that do need some review and are of concern to negotiations between management and labour in many circumstances. The precision of the wording indicates a basic knowledge and understanding of the effects of the labour code, both positive and negative. Again, I congratulate the member for Richelieu for bringing this forward.
The main thrust of the bill is that it is anti-scab labour. It is against the opportunity of hiring scab labour. In other words, it does not allow the bringing in of strikebreakers. The implication of the previous speaker was that this was in place, but it is not in place. If an employer wants to use management to keep the operation going, that is well within the structure of the present code. The code has allowed the bringing in of strikebreakers under certain circumstances. This bill would
Private Members' Business
limit that entirely, and that is the basic direction of the bill.
I cannot argue against that. I think it is a necessary change to the labour code and should be supported by all people in the House who have some concerns about the quality of labour and management relations. This bill would balance the power of the two groups a little more.
There is a second section to this bill with which I had some concern. The second section uses language which gives to the cabinet or the Governor in Council that which those of us who have worked near, with and beside, and in some cases against labour unions recognize as giving power which they have not had in the the past but would get under this bill. Consequently it would be less acceptable than it might have been without those changes in the wording.
I refer to sections 90.3 and 90.9. section 90.3 deals with the establishment of essential services. This is not too objectionable in that it does establish a negotiation process between the union and the employer before it gives power to the cabinet or the Governor in Council to take action.
Section 100 fractures the structure that we have known and accepted as the basic structure of the negotiation process. What it does is give to the cabinet the power to disallow a strike.
My point is if you certify a union, you accept its structure and its operations. It has the right to strike and it operates as a union in the negotiating process. The minister may suddenly say: "Under a particular circumstance this particular union will not be able to strike". All of us in this House have been brought back on occasion, working either for or against the passage of a bill to put people back to work. We passed one not too long, Bill C-49. That process has worked in the past. The reason for the back-to-work is brought forward publicly and discussed. That is an adequate process. Section 100, which gives this power to the Governor in Council under certain circumstances, is degrading the process of negotiation as far as the union and employer is concerned.
I appreciate the fact that this brings in a kind of anti-scab, anti-strikebreaker legislation. It deals effectively with the establishment of essential services. There is one concern which should be dealt with in a legislative committee, that is to allow cabinet power to eliminate the possibility of a strike under certain circumstances,

May 31, 1990
Private Members' Business
power which the cabinet does not now have. Therefore, I say that is an unacceptable approach.
I also have concern as to the breadth of it, the fact that it is limited under certain circumstances. This is the kind of anti-strikebreaker legislation which we think should be an across-the-board code and should be available as protection to employees in all kinds of industries.
I hope that when this bill passes second reading, it goes to a legislative committee that will look at the wording, the concern as far as power that the cabinet has with the wording and to give the unions and employers, the corporations, the ability to come before the committee and say: "Yes, we agree," or "No, we disagree with certain parts of it." We can then bring forth better legislation than we might otherwise.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ken James (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   CANADA LABOUR CODE MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to join the debate on the proposed legislation before us, Bill C-201, an act to amend the Canada Labour Code.
As has been discussed, this bill is targeted at federal Crown corporations which fall within the jurisdiction of the Code and provides for a prohibition on the hiring of replacement workers during work stoppage, and also that essential services would be maintained in the event of a work stoppage in a Crown corporation specifically.
The bill contains interesting proposals but also raises some questions. One question arising from the proposed legislation is that it seeks to change the current industrial relations system in existence under Part I of the Code at a time when the current procedures appear to be functioning quite well. I hope hon. members will not interpret the introduction of Bill C-201 as meaning that the present framework for collective bargaining under Part I is not working. In fact, figures from the federal jurisdiction indicate that the settlement rate for cases handled to the final stage without resort to work stoppage action remains above 90 per cent. In addition, the reliance on formal third party intervention in labour disputes at the conciliation commission level has decreased very dramatically over recent years, with only one case accorded such assistance during the 1989-90 fiscal year.
The figures I have quoted reflect a philosophy and a continuing commitment toward promoting a responsible and responsive bargaining framework. The policy is designed to encourage the parties, with their intimate knowledge of the issues in dispute, to resolve their own differences and conclude a mutually satisfactory collective agreement. As hon. members will appreciate, an agreement concluded by the parties themselves is much preferable to one forced upon them through arbitration or some other statutory means.
If I may for a moment, I would like to briefly review the provisions currently found within Part I of the Canada Labour Code. Part I of the Code establishes the framework for industrial relations and regulates the conduct of collective bargaining in the federal private sector. This jurisdiction covers the operations of enterprises that fall within the definition of a "federal work, undertaking or business" and includes interprovincial and international rail, road and pipeline transportation, air transportation, shipping, longshoring, grain handling, banking, broadcasting, and certain Crown corporations.
The Canada Labour Code requires that the conciliation process be exhausted before the legal right to strike or lockout can be exercised. Normally, this process involves the appointment of a conciliation officer, but it may also involve the additional efforts of a conciliation commissioner or conciliation board. Following the termination of conciliation and the acquisition of the right to strike or lockout, the minister may appoint a mediator to further assist the parties in negotiations.
As I indicated earlier in my remarks, the use of the more formal conciliation commissioner option has decreased in past years with an increasing onus being placed on the parties themselves to deal directly with the issues and not look to shift the responsibility for settlement to an outside third party. I understand that in those cases where a dispute is not settled at the conciliation officer stage and the repercussions of a work stoppage would have serious economic consequences, the situation is weighed carefully before a decision as to the appointment of additional assistants is taken.
It is however of interest to note that while the use of the commissioner option has decreased, the settlement rate without work stoppage in the federal jurisdiction has
May 31, 1990

remained in the 90 per cent range and the incidence of work stoppages has remained relatively stable.
An excellent example of this renewed reliance, which the Minister of Labour is placing on the parties to deal with the issues in dispute and arrive at acceptable compromises, was the most recent contract settlement involving the grain handlers in the port of Thunder Bay.
Negotiations between the Transportation and Communications International Union, Lodge 650, and Lakehead terminal elevators to renew the collective agreement which expired on January 31, 1988 received the assistance of a conciliation officer from Labour Canada over a 10-month period before the talks broke down.
After a careful assessment of the various factors involved in the negotiations and of the economic impact of a work stoppage at that point in time, a decision not to appoint a conciliation commissioner was taken. The parties were notified of the decision and some weeks later resumed direct negotiations. These proved successful and a tentative settlement was reached which was subsequently ratified by the union membership.
Another situation in which the onus was directed back to the parties to deal with matters in dispute arose in the 1989 negotiations between the Council of Marine Carriers and the Canadian Merchant Service Guild representing tow boat employees on the west coast. Again, the parties were initially assisted in their discussions by a conciliation officer over a four-month period.
However, bargaining broke off and the Minister of Labour was faced with a decision as to whether further assistance in the form of a conciliation commissioner should be provided. Following a thorough assessment of this situation, it was decided that a conciliation commissioner would not be appointed to the dispute. Instead, the assistance of a mediator from Labour Canada, fully versed in the issues in dispute, was provided to the parties and a tentative settlement was arrived at shortly thereafter in the mediation proceedings.
Private Members' Business
Another concern which I have about the proposed bill before us relates to what might be termed a piecemeal approach to dealing with legislative amendments to this very important code. Part I of the Labour Canada Code has proven over the years to be a fair and equitable statute in dealing with industrial relations in the federal jurisdiction and has like most federal legislation periodically undergone extensive review and evaluation.
What the hon. member is proposing through Bill C-21 deals with only one specific segment of the federal jurisdiction universe, namely Crown corporations, and with issues which are complex in nature such as essential services.
I would suggest that changes such as those proposed in the bill before us should be considered as part of the total review of Part I of the Canada Labour Code and not in isolation from the other provisions of the legislation. What we have here is a proposal from the hon. member to amend comprehensive labour relations legislation in order to deal with certain concerns specific to a particular segment of the total federal jurisdiction universe.
In dealing with the topic of replacement workers, I should point out that we should study this particular legislation to some extent before voting.
